Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 1:

(p-101) The surah of "al-Nahl" (The Bee)

Its purpose is to demonstrate that He (Exalted is He) is perfect in power and knowledge, acts by choice, and is free from any taint of deficiency. The clearest indication of this meaning in it is the matter of the bee, because of what it mentions of the bee's precise understanding in arranging its hives, its grazing, and all its affairs, including the variety of colours of the honey that comes out of it, His making it a cure, its eating of beneficial and harmful fruits, and other matters. Its being described as a bounty is clear in this. And God knows best.

"In the name of God" (bismillah), who encompasses the circle of perfection, so whatever He wills He does. "The Most Gracious" (al-Rahman), whose bounty has embraced His creation, the great and the small, the lowly and the high. "The Most Merciful" (al-Rahim), who singles out whom He wills with the bounty of deliverance from what displeases Him, through what pleases Him.

When He concluded al-Hijr with an allusion to the coming of certainty (al-yaqin), which is suitable for the death of all and for the lifting of the veil through the coming of what they are promised and what they seek to hasten in mockery of the punishment (p-102) in the Hereafter, after what they meet in this world, He began this surah in the same manner, except that He concluded that one with the name of the Lord, which implies kindness, out of gentleness toward the one addressed, and He began this one with the Greatest Name, which comprises all the meanings of the names, because that is more fitting to the situation of threat, and because of the varied meanings you will come to know in the course of the surah. This name will be repeated in it many times, by which the soundness of this claim will be known. He expressed what is to come in the past tense, indicating its certainty, as certain as what has already occurred and passed, and that every coming thing is necessarily near. So He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿The command of God has come﴾; that is, the Mighty King, to whom belong the most beautiful names and the highest attributes, with that which humbles the enemies, honours the friends, heals their breasts, and comforts their eyes.

Since haste is a deficiency, He said, making this report the cause: ﴿So do not seek to hasten it﴾; O enemies, in mockery; and O friends, seeking sufficiency and healing. This is like what the conjunction in His saying (Exalted is He) implied: ﴿And We did not destroy any town but that it had a decreed term﴾ [al-Hijr: 4], as has preceded. The pronoun may refer to God, or to the command.

Since the affirmation of future matters is not fitting except when the command is executed, and execution belongs only to one who has no equal, and since haste, which is bringing a thing before its appointed time, is a manifest deficiency that is attributed only to narrowness of understanding, and since delay occurs only on account of a rival partner, He declared Himself absolutely free of these, comprehensively, by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Glory be to Him﴾; that is, He is exalted above haste and above all attributes of deficiency; ﴿and exalted﴾; that is, of very great exaltation; ﴿above what they associate﴾; that is, what they claim as a partner to Him. Therefore nothing hinders what He wills to do. He expressed this in the third person in other than the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, to show disregard, which indicates intense anger. It refers back to His saying at the end of the preceding surah: ﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾ [al-Hijr: 94], and His saying: ﴿who set up with God another god﴾ [al-Hijr: 96]. The matter in the arrangement of the verse has come to be as if it were said: He does not hasten, because He is free of deficiency, and His command must be carried out, because He is exalted above having an equal. Or it may be said: Do not seek to hasten Him, for He is free of deficiency and so does not hasten; and He is exalted above having any equal who could repel what He wills, so it must come to pass. Thus this is in the position of a causal explanation for the opening of the verse, just as the opening of the verse is a causal explanation for the end of the surah of al-Hijr.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 2:

When this has been established, His transcendence above every deficiency, whether associating partners with Him or anything else, He (glory be to Him) began to describe Himself with attributes of perfection, [namely] of command (amr) and creation (khalq). Since command is more ancient and more exalted, He began with it. And since among His command is the sending down of the angels in the form they requested in their saying: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ [al-Hijr: 7], and He recounted to them in the surahs of Ibrahim and Lut, peace be upon them both, what follows from their descent in a gathered manner, it is understood from this that in their descent they have another state, which the messengers do not deny, namely the state of coming to them with knowledge, whose relation to spirits is the relation of spirits to bodies. This might have raised for them an objection, by which they seek to distinguish themselves from the messengers in the descent of the angels upon them rather than upon the messengers, as has preceded in "al-Hijr." And what they associate with Him has no power at all, neither in descent nor in anything else. He (exalted be He), pointing to that, and to the fact that revelation is through the mediation of an angel, and that prophethood is a bestowal and not an acquisition, said: ﴿He sends down the angels﴾, who are the exalted assembly; ﴿with the Spirit﴾, that is, the greatest meaning, which for spirits stands in the position that spirits stand in for bodies; ﴿by His command﴾, which is His speech comprising command and prohibition; ﴿Surely to Him belong creation and command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. It is among what He is distinguished by, because of its truth and its inimitability, above all created things; so how much more so are things that have no intellect among them, such as idols? ﴿upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾, not upon others, because that is the result of His acting by choice. He made "the Spirit" a substitute (badal), or explained the sending down as revelation, because it includes the meaning of speech, so He said: ﴿that warn﴾, that is, warn the people of My punishments, for they will surely descend upon whomever I intend to bring them down upon; ﴿that there is no god but I﴾. He expressed it with the first-person pronoun because it is more indicative of the intended meaning, owing to its being more definite. And He derived from His oneness, which is the furthest point of the perfection of the theoretical faculty, His saying, commanding what is the utmost perfection of the practical faculty: ﴿so fear Me﴾, that is, let your fear of Me be intense, and let your taking of what serves as a protection for you from My punishment be firm; for there is no hindrance to what I intend. Whomever I know to be deserving of retribution, I send it down upon him; and whomever I know to be fit to receive the Spirit, I grant it to him.

(p-106) When He declared His own oneness, He indicated this by His saying, explaining His bringing into existence the roots and branches of the world in a manner of wisdom: ﴿He created the heavens﴾, that is, which are the canopy that shades; ﴿and the earth﴾, that is, which is the spread that bears; ﴿with truth﴾, that is, with a matter that is established and firm, not with deception and imagination; ﴿Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54].

When that was among the attributes of perfection, which entail the negation of deficiencies, and when it was decisive in exalting Him above having a partner, because if there were one, it would follow that opposition is possible, and so inability to achieve the intended outcome, or the existence of two opposing wills each intending contrary things, and each of these is impossible; so the existence of a partner is impossible. And because both of them, and all that is in them, are His possession and under His control, and there is no dispute for whoever affirms God in that, He followed it with His saying, as a conclusion from that, indicating that He (exalted) is not of the category of bodies: ﴿Exalted is He﴾, that is, an exaltation that exceeds description; ﴿above what they associate with Him﴾, diverging from beginning it with exaltation as in the first.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 4:

Since the creation of the heavens and the earth is unseen (ghayb), because it preceded (the human being), and the creation of man in this condition is something witnessed (shahadah), and moreover it is more indicative of that (the Creator's power) in that man is more noble than everything that is worshipped besides God, and the Lord can never be lower than the servant at all—He said, giving the reason: ﴿He created man﴾; that is, this species, whose creation is the strongest indication of the Oneness (of God) and of acting by choice. This is because he is the most noble of what exists in the lower world of bodies, through sharing with the animal (which is nobler than others) in the noble faculties of the outer and inner senses, and in appetite and anger, and through being singled out for speech, which is the apprehension of universals and the manipulation of them through syllogisms. ﴿From a drop of semen﴾; that is, Adam—peace be upon him—from water in its absolute sense, and whoever descended from him after his spouse from water restricted to a gushing emission.

And since man, despite sharing with the other animals in being created from a drop of semen, is distinguished by speech, which rests upon the wonders of craftsmanship within him and the subtleties of perception, this is the clearest evidence of the perfect power of the Agent and of His choice. Thus He (exalted) said: ﴿Then behold, he﴾; that is, the man created from despicable water, ﴿is an open disputer﴾; that is, eloquent, skilled in argument, ﴿clear﴾; that is, manifestly capable of contention, and clarifying what he intends to the utmost clarity, after having been something with no sensation at all, and no voluntary movement in any way. Will not He who began that be able to restore it?!

[p. 108]

When *tawhid* (the affirmation of God's oneness) became, by this, as clear as the sun, and since everything in the universe, although it itself points to God's oneness, is a blessing upon man for which he is obliged to give thanks, [al-Biqa'i] began to enumerate these blessings, as an alert to him about the obligation of gratitude through disavowing disbelief. He said, giving precedence to the animals because they are nobler than other things, and giving precedence among them to those that benefit man because he is more excellent than others, beginning with what is first in mention because it is the greatest in benefit for the necessities of livelihood and the most binding upon those to whom the Remembrance was revealed in their own tongue: ﴿And the cattle He created for you﴾. That is, the eight pairs: sheep, goats, camels and cattle. ﴿He created them﴾, not speaking and not clear [in speech], although they are greater than you in creation and stronger in might.

When the first of their blessings that a person usually encounters is clothing, [God] began with it, saying, by way of resumption: ﴿For you in them is warmth﴾. That is, that by which one is warmed, so that there is from it a moderate heat from the warmth of the body, produced by wrapping, which keeps off the cold. He then followed this with what encompasses all their blessings, among which is milk, saying: ﴿and [other] benefits﴾. Then He made it a third by [mentioning] eating, since it comes after that, saying (exalted is He): ﴿and from them you eat﴾. He placed the prepositional phrase first, to indicate that eating from other than them, in comparison with eating from them, is not considered worthy of account.

Then He followed it with adornment, because it is the culmination, since it belongs to men. So He said (Exalted is He): ﴿And for you﴾; that is, O people, exclusively; ﴿in them﴾; that is, the livestock (al-An'am); ﴿is beauty﴾; that is, great beauty.

And since the coming home (al-qudum) is a greater blessing and more delightful than the departure (al-nuzuh), He placed it first, saying: ﴿when you bring them home﴾ in the evening from the pastures, and they are large of udders and long of humps; ﴿and when you drive them out﴾ in the morning from the pens (al-marah) to the pastures. So in these two states there is, for them (the animals), movements of various kinds, from themselves and from their herders, and from milking, and from going back and forth for it, and the answering of bleating and lowing is a great matter and a considerable source of companionship for their owners.

Since the journeys came after that, He followed it with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And they carry﴾; that is, the cattle; ﴿your loads﴾; that is, your goods; along with hardship; ﴿to a land﴾; that is, other than your land, to which you intended to travel; ﴿which you could not have reached﴾; that is, in a state for which you were naturally made, able to carry them there; and [He] conveys you, by carrying them for you, to a land which you could not ﴿reach﴾ without the camels; ﴿except with great hardship﴾; that is, with effort, difficulty and burden ﴿to yourselves﴾. It is also possible that the meaning is: you would not have reached it by them; so how would it be if they did not exist? The word "shiqq" (half, here used in the sense of a half-portion) means one of the two halves of a thing; it seems to be a metaphor for the loss of half of one's strength because of the exertion that befalls a person. The verse is of the type called ihtibak (interweaving): it mentions the carrying of loads first, as an indication of the carrying of souls second; and it mentions the hardship of reaching the destination second, as an indication of the hardship of carrying first.

Since all of this is part of the kindness in provision, and no one subjects a creature to the weak except one who is abundant in mercy, and since among people there are those for whom some of their deeds are a cause of their Lord's pleasure, and among them are those whose deeds are all corrupt (p-110), He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord﴾; that is, the One who brought you into being and who is good to you; ﴿is most Kind﴾; that is, abundantly merciful toward whoever seeks access to Him by what pleases Him; ﴿Merciful﴾; that is, abundantly merciful, whether there is a cause or not.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 8:

Since livestock constituted most of their wealth, and their benefits were greater, He began with them. Then He followed with what is inferior to them, arranging it according to rank, from the most noble to the next most noble. So He said (Exalted is He): ﴿And horses﴾, i.e., the neighing ones; ﴿and mules﴾, i.e., those born of crossing between them [the horses] and the donkeys; ﴿and donkeys﴾, i.e., the braying ones.

Since riding was an act of those addressed, and it is what is intended by the benefit, He mentioned it with the lam, which is the original particle of causation, saying: ﴿that you may ride them﴾. And since adornment follows from benefit, and was an act of the doer of the causative act, it was put in the accusative as a conjunction with the position of what precedes it, so He said: ﴿and as adornment﴾.

Since He indicated His power by what He mentioned in the context of bestowing favour, He indicated that these [blessings] are not limited to that context. So He drew attention to the fact that He created for them matters which, had He enumerated them, they would not have understood the intended meaning of, because of their ignorance of them. Perhaps these are greater benefits than what was mentioned. So He said: ﴿And He creates﴾, i.e., by way of renewal and continuity, in this world (p-111) and the Hereafter, ﴿what you do not know﴾. So you know of no originator for it other than Him, nor any governor besides Him.

(p-111) When they were travelling and seeking benefit from these animals and others, they aimed for the easiest, straightest and most direct routes to their goal. Whoever deviated from this was considered by them to be misguided, feeble-minded, and unworthy of being counted among the noble. He (Allah) alerted them that what preceded in this surah had already clarified the straightest path that leads to Him, glorified is He, by making clear that He is One, Capable, Knowing, and Choosing, and that He is the Bestower of blessings, so worship must be devoted to Him alone. He, glorified is He, informed them that He had made this clarification incumbent upon Himself, out of bounty from Him. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And upon Allah﴾, meaning: He has already made clear to you the way. And upon ﴿Allah﴾, meaning the One who has encompassing knowledge of everything, ﴿is the directing of the way﴾, meaning: the clarification of the right, upright path. Upon Allah is also the clarification of the deviating path, so that no doubt remains about either of them. For the paths of meaning are like the sensible paths: among them is the straight one, which whoever follows is guided; ﴿and among them is the deviating one﴾, whoever follows it strays from reaching the destination and so is ruined. ﴿And Allah would not lead a people astray after He had guided them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 115], and so on; ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15]. This verse is an instance of ihtibak (interlocking ellipsis): He mentioned that upon Him is the clarification of the directing of the way first, indicating the omission that upon Him is the clarification of the deviating path second; and He mentioned that among the paths is the deviating one second, indicating the omission that among them is the straight one first. The expression is used to show that the primary intent is the clarification of what is beneficial. The root *q-ṣ-d* revolves around equity and evenness, and from it comes *al-qaṣd*, meaning rectitude, the straightness of a path without deviation, and the opposite of excess, like *al-iqtiṣād* (moderation). One says of a man who is neither large nor small: *laysa bi-l-jasīm wa-lā bi-l-ḍa'īl* (he is neither bulky nor slight). This does not happen except through will and direction. Therefore the application of *qaṣd* to resolve (ʿazm), whether straight or deviating, when you say *qaṣadtuhu* meaning "I came to him," or "I aimed at him," or "I intended him," is by implication (dalālat al-iltizām). Likewise *al-qaṣd* in the sense of "breaking," in whatever manner, is so; and it has been said: *qaṣada* is not said except when the break is in the middle. *Al-qaṣīd* is a poem whose half-verses are complete, because that is its most balanced state. Al-Fayruzabadi said in the *Qamus*: three verses or more, or sixteen verses or more. The Imam Abu al-Fath ʿUthman ibn Jinni said at the end of his book *al-Maghrib fi Sharh al-Qawafi*: the verse is of three types: short (qasir), ramal, and rajaz. As for the *qaṣīd*, it is the complete ṭawīl (a complete meter of the long type), the complete basīṭ, the complete kāmil, the complete madīd, the complete wāfir, the complete rajaz, and the complete khafīf, and this is everything that riders sing. Our saying "complete madid" and "complete wafir" (p-112) means the most complete form of these that occurs in usage, that is, the first two of their patterns. As for their occurring in the original form of their circles, that is rejected and discarded. *Al-qaṣīd* is also thick marrow or what is less than that, a bone full of marrow, a fat she-camel with fat in her, and the fat part of the humps, because in this state every one of the things mentioned attains its rectitude. Likewise *al-qāṣid* means near, and "between us and the water is a near night" means an easy journey, because it is closer to straightness. From this comes "I aimed at such-and-such" when I resolved upon it, intended it, and turned toward it, whether that was just or unjust. And *inqaṣada al-rumḥ* (the spear broke) when it broke, in the same sense, as though it were the one submitting to the action of breaking; and one piece of those breaks is *qiṣda* (with kasra); and *rumḥ qaṣid* like *katif* means broken. *Al-qaṣad* with a fatha on the middle letter means the thornbush ʿawsaj, because it breaks quickly; and hunger, because the hungry person is intent on what he eats and directed toward it. *Al-qaṣad* also means the young shoots of the trees ʿiḍāh: they come out in the autumn days as supple shoots that bend at the ends of the branches; it is a leaf bud that emerges in them and in many trees during those days; or it means the branches themselves, or the moist branches before they change color and harden; they were so named because of their emergence and their turning toward the view of the eye, or the turning of the gaze toward them for the joy of them. *Al-qaṣīd* also means a staff, because it is aimed at and used as a target. *Aqṣada al-sahm* means the arrow hit and killed on the spot; *aqṣada fulānan* means he stabbed him and did not miss him. *Al-ḥayya* (the snake) when it bites and kills is also so; this can be from rectitude, because the purpose of its doer is killing, so it is as though its intention was made straight by its reaching its target; and it can be from negation, meaning it removed rectitude, because whoever dies has lost the straightness of his life. From this comes *al-maqṣad*, like *mukhraj*, meaning one who falls ill and dies quickly. *Al-qaṣīd*, in the sense of dried meat, is a form *faʿīl* in the sense of *mufʿal*, meaning it was made to be aimed at and its rectitude was removed, by perishing through dryness and desiccation.

*Al-ṣidq* (truthfulness) is the opposite of lying, and it is among the most equitable of equity and the most upright of the directions. *Al-ṣidq* also means firmness, for through it the truthful is distinguished from the liar. From this comes *rajul ṣidq*, meaning a man who makes true what he resolves upon or says through his deed; so he is of firm resolve and sound judgment. *Al-ṣadīq*, like *amīr*, is the beloved who confirms his words of love by a deed. *Al-muṣādaqa* and *al-ṣidāq* (with kasra) mean friendship, like *al-taṣādduq*. *Al-ṣaydaq*, like *ṣayqal*, is the trustworthy one, because he is believed in what he says; and the king, because his position requires truthfulness, since he has no need to lie; and the pole (of the sky), because it is the most truthful of the stars in indication by its steadiness. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Qazzaz said it is a name for *al-Suhā*, the faint star that is with the Bananat Naʿsh (Ursa Major). *Al-ṣadq* with a fatha means the hard, straight spears, because it confirmed the expectation of the one who thrust with it; and likewise among men; and the perfect of everything. A man of *ṣidq* al-liqāʾ wa-l-naẓar means truthful in encounter and in gaze. *Miṣdāq al-shayʾ* is what confirms it. *Shujāʿ dhū miṣdaq*, like *minbar*, means one whose charge is true, that is, its strength. *Al-ṣadaqa* (with fatha on the middle letter) is what you give for the sake of Allah, because it confirms the claim of faith, by indicating the intensity of resolve in it. *Al-ṣadqa* (with damma or sukun on the middle letter) is a woman's dowry, because the resolve in it is true. Like *sikkīt*, it means one who is very truthful. *Ṣadaqtu Allāh ḥadīthan in lam afʿal kadhā* (I swear by Allah that I will not do such-and-such) is an oath for them, meaning "no, I did not." *Faʿalahu ghibba ṣādiqa*, meaning after the matter became clear to him. *Ṣaddaqahu taṣdīqan* is the opposite of *kadhdhabahu* (he confirmed him, the opposite of he called him a liar). *Al-waḥshī* (the wild animal) when it runs and does not turn toward what chased it. *Al-muṣaddaq*, like *muḥdath*, means the one who takes the alms. *Al-mutaṣaddiq* means the one who gives them.

Since the majority of creation is astray, one might imagine that someone is outside the will (of Allah). So He negated this illusion by His saying, coordinated with what is implied as: "So whoever He wills, He guides to the straight path, and whoever He wills, He leads along the deviating path," and He is capable of what He wills (p-113) of guidance and misguidance: ﴿And if He had willed﴾, your guidance, ﴿He would have guided you all﴾, by creating guidance in your hearts after making the straight path clear; but He did not will that, so He made you into two groups.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 10:

Since what had preceded was sufficient to demonstrate that He is the One who chooses (al-Wahid al-Mukhtar), he began to clarify this by detailing the signs with a clarity that leaves it in the fullest disclosure, within a context that enumerates the blessings, reminds of them, and calls to gratitude for them. So he said, after having indicated by the human being, and what follows him in nobility among the animals, beginning with what follows them in nobility among the plants, which is the foundation of human life, and what human life is sustained by among the animals: ﴿He﴾, not other than Him, of whom divinity is claimed, ﴿is the One who sent down﴾, that is, by His overpowering might, ﴿from the sky﴾. It was said: from the sky itself. It was said: from its direction. It was said: from the clouds, as is observed. ﴿Water﴾, that is, one kind, which you perceive by taste and by sight. ﴿For you from it﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿is drink﴾, apparent upon the face of the earth, from springs, rivers, pools, and others.

Since the first thing that sustains the human being is milk, which arises from water, he placed it first. He followed it with what arises from it, the most noble of his foods, which is the animal product. So He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And from it is a tree﴾, because it permeates the single earth and mixes with it, so that a plant grows from that. ﴿In which you pasture [your animals]﴾, that is, you let them graze freely, by night and by day, the livestock He created for you. The word "shajar" (tree) here, as conveyed by the sense of al-isama (free pasturing of livestock), is general: it covers what remains through the winter in the strict sense, and other things in a figurative sense. Al-Qazzaz said: "shajar" is that which keeps a stem through the winter until the summer, then bears leaves again; and "baql" (herbage) is that which does not keep a stem. Al-Khalil said: "jill al-shajar" is its large parts, and what remains of it in winter; and its "diqq" (small parts) are of two kinds. One of them keeps a root (arumah) in the earth through the winter and sprouts in spring; and among it is what sprouts from the earth as herbage does. The distinction between it and baql is that the shajar keeps a root through the winter, while baql does not keep one. On the authority of Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him), plants are of three kinds: shajar, which is what remains in winter and whose branch and root do not perish; what grows from a seed and does not grow from a firm root, which is baql; and what grows from a root, that is, a base, and is of the kind whose branch and root perish in winter, which is the janba (intermediate type), since it is distinct from the shajar whose branch and root remain, and from the baql whose branch and root are destroyed; so it was an intermediate between them.

When the trees were mentioned in general terms, He (glorified be He) began to specify them, both to vary the blessings and to remind us of the differences among them, pointing out that the act is by choice. So He said, beginning with the most beneficial in terms of sustenance, condiment and fruit:

﴿He causes to grow﴾, that is, He (glorified be He); ﴿for you﴾, that is, specifically for you; ﴿by it﴾, despite its being one water in one land; ﴿the crops﴾, which you see, from among the trees of least duration and smallest size; ﴿and the olives﴾, which you see, from among the longest-lived and greatest in size of trees.

Since the benefits of the date palm are many, He named it by its own name and said (exalted is He): ﴿and the date palms﴾. Since the benefit of the vine apart from its fruit is slight, He said (exalted is He): ﴿and the grapevines﴾. These two are of the middle of that category. ﴿And of all the fruits﴾. As for all of them, they exist only in Paradise, and what is on the earth is a part of that whole, reminding of it and stirring longing for it.

﴿Surely in that﴾, that is, in the great water spoken of, and in its branches, or in its sending down in the described manner, ﴿is a sign﴾, clear, that the one who does this has perfect power, able to bring back as He originated, and that He is one who chooses, doing that at the time He wills.

Since this is something perceived by the senses, and since occupation of the senses with its benefit, owing to its nearness and ease of contact, may often distract from reflection on what is meant by it, and since noticing its indication requires extra contemplation and fine observation, He said (exalted is He): ﴿for a people who reflect﴾, that is, on the fact that its unity, and the multitude of what branches from it, is evidence of the unity of its Maker and of His acting by choice. He used the singular "sign" because of the unity of what it is produced from, namely water, as He said (exalted is He) in the verse: ﴿It is watered with one water﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4]. The statement of the Imam Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali on this will come in the commentary on the verse of al-Nahl.

The Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: This surah's connection with the surah of al-Hijr is like the connection of al-Hijr with the surah of Ibrahim, without any gap. When He (exalted is He) said: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92], ﴿about what they used to do﴾ [al-Hijr: 93], and He said after that, in the threat against the mockers: ﴿but they will come to know﴾ [al-Hijr: 96], He followed this with an explanation of the hastening of the matter, saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. He added to this explanation His words: ﴿Glorified and exalted is He above what they associate﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. Thus He declared Himself free of what they uttered in their mockery and their polytheism and their enormous slander, and He followed this with declaring Him free and exalting Him, saying: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth; exalted is He above what they associate﴾ [al-Nahl: 3]. Then He followed this with mention of the beginning of the creation of man and the weakness of his nature: ﴿He created man from a drop of fluid﴾ [al-Nahl: 4]. Then He brought him to a state in which there is contention and argument. All of this is a trial from Him and a test, so that He may distinguish the wicked from the good. He followed this with mention of some of His kindnesses in the creation of livestock, and the various benefits He placed in them, and His compassion and mercy, by which He delayed punishment from those who deserved it and guided those who did not deserve guidance in themselves. Indeed every guidance is by the kindness and mercy of the Creator. Then He followed what He had mentioned afterwards, of the creation of horses, mules and donkeys, and all that is in that, with His words: ﴿And if He willed, He would have guided you all﴾ [al-Nahl: 9]. Thus He made clear that all that occurs, of guidance and misguidance, is His creation and His act, and that He brought all into being from one origin and began them with one beginning: ﴿He created man from a drop of fluid﴾ [al-Nahl: 4]. So there is no strangeness in the difference of their ends after that. He has shown us, (exalted is He), an example of this act and its counterpart in His words: ﴿It is He who sent down water from the sky, from which you have drink and from which come trees﴾ [al-Nahl: 10], up to His words: ﴿Surely in that is a sign for a people who reflect﴾. The end.

(p-121) Since some of the misguided might say that these things depend on the influence of the celestial spheres (al-aflak), He drew attention to the fact that they are not fit for that, because they are subject to change. Therefore there must be a dominant agent that caused the change in them; and the matter continues thus until it ends at one who is eternal and acts by choice (bi'l-ikhtiyar), because the impossibility of an infinite regress (tasalsul) has been established. So He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And He has made subservient for you﴾; that is, O people, for the improvement of your conditions; ﴿the night﴾ for rest; ﴿and the day﴾ for seeking (provision). Then He mentioned the sign of the day, saying (exalted is He): ﴿and the sun﴾; that is, for benefits which He reserved for it; then He mentioned the sign of the night, saying: ﴿and the moon﴾, for matters He attached to it; ﴿and the stars﴾; that is, as signs He set up for them. Then He drew attention to their change by His saying: ﴿subservient by His command﴾; that is, with various kinds of change, for the purpose for which He created them, in the arrangements He ordered; ﴿by His command﴾, as a means for your welfare and the welfare of that by which your livelihood is sustained; as evidence of His oneness and of His acting by choice. Had He willed, He would have established other causes than these, or dispensed with causes altogether.

Since their affair — despite being perceptible — does not contain benefits that are near at hand and easily encountered that would distract from reflection upon it, He did not leave its matter to anything other than pure intellect, as an indication of its clarity; though it necessarily requires the use of the reflective faculty. And because the heavenly phenomena are more indicative of the overwhelming power and more manifest a testimony to majesty and greatness, He said: ﴿Indeed in that﴾; that is, in this great subjugation (al-taskhir) (p-122) ﴿are signs﴾; that is, many, multiple, great; ﴿for a people who reason﴾. He used the plural "signs" (ayat) because their enumeration becomes evident through speaking of them in detail.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 13:

Since what has passed was a place for reflection that yields knowledge of the Creator's oneness and His choice, and since reflecting on that reminds one of what follows, namely the secret of variation in colour, whose kinds cannot be fully enumerated, and since in that there is complete refutation of the claim that the spheres (al-aflak) and natures (al-tabai') have the influence, because their relation to all the parts of a single leaf and a single seed is one and the same, He, exalted is He, said, coordinating it with "the night" (al-layl): ﴿And what He has created﴾, i.e. He created, scattered, and dispersed the earth and water, ﴿for you﴾, i.e. specifically, so give thanks to Him, and know that He has not singled you out with this great arrangement except for great wisdoms, the most important of which is the manifestation of His majesty on the Day of Decision; ﴿in the earth﴾, i.e. among what was mentioned and other than it, while ﴿its colours are diverse﴾, even within a single leaf, so you see one of its two faces, or part of it, in the utmost redness, and the other in the utmost blackness, or yellowness, and the like. Had the agent been one that acts by necessity in its essence, this variation in effects would be impossible, so it is known with certainty that He is only capable and choosing. He did not mention (p-123) the diversity of forms, because its indication, owing to the differing shapes of the stars in the sky and the forms of mountains, hills and valleys on the earth, is not a proof against nature in the way that the diversity of colour is.

Since that, although it exceeds limits in its spread, is one in respect of being a colour, He made the sign singular and said: ﴿Indeed in that﴾, which He created in this state, in this great manner, ﴿is a sign﴾. And since in the preceding verse He alerted that the matter had reached such clarity that nothing beyond the immediate judgement of reason is needed, here He alerted that this is known yet is subject to forgetfulness and heedlessness, urging the effort of contemplating it and indicating that its indication of the intended meaning is in the utmost clarity. So He said: ﴿for a people who remember﴾, even if they do not exert themselves, by what the idgham (assimilation) conveys. And "tadhakkur" (remembrance): seeking meaning by reflecting upon its object, so there must be the presence of a meaning by which something else is sought. He, glorified is He, arranged this in the most wondrous order: He first mentioned composite bodies in general, then singled out living beings, then the absolute growing body, which is plants, then the simple elements, such as water and the like, then the accidents, such as colours.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 14:

When He (glory be to Him) had shown His power and His free choice, as an indication of His capacity over everything He had informed of, especially the Hour, by the creation of the heavens and the earth, which is greater than the creation of mankind, He then mentioned some of what is in the visible earth, surrounded by air, of variation that indicates the uniqueness of the Maker and His choice, and He concluded it with colour. He followed that with what is submerged in water, which in reality has no colour, indicating that it contains, among the benefits and animals that have quantities, qualities, shapes and colours of wonderfully varied drawing and strangely varied dyeing, what is even more indicative than that. So He said: ﴿And it is He﴾; that is, none other than Him; ﴿who subjected the sea﴾; that is, made it submissive and prepared it for the living of what is in it of animals, the formation of jewels, and other benefits. What is meant by it is the seven seas situated in the quarter of the earth raised above the water, which is the inhabited part of the globe of the earth, drawn from the encompassing sea that covers three-quarters of the earth. He made it, by subjection, such that people are able to benefit from it by riding, diving and other things. ﴿That you may eat from it﴾; that is, by fishing and otherwise, from the flesh of fish; ﴿fresh flesh﴾; you find nothing more pleasant or tender than it; it is the moistest of flesh, so decay quickly sets in, and it is hastened to be eaten sweet and delicious, though it is born in salty brine; ﴿and that you may extract from it﴾; that is, by your effort in diving and what follows from it; ﴿ornaments that you wear﴾ [that is, your women, who are part of you, so that the wearer is in effect you], and they are of stones harder and purer than which none is seen, namely pearls, and likewise coral and other things; together with the attribution of this hardness and that freshness to water, for if it were acting by its nature, they would be alike.

When He had mentioned the general benefits, addressing them with them, and the plowing (al-makhr, i.e., a ship advancing against the wind, cutting the water so that a pleasing sound is heard from its passage, and that with a heavy load) was a great sign which only people of hearts contemplate, He singled out with the address the most eminent of people of intellect and those who approach them in seeking what is right, saying: ﴿And you see the ships﴾; and since looking at the enumeration of blessings here is more complete than in the surah of "Fatir," He placed the makhr in His saying: ﴿plowing through it﴾; that is, running ships cutting the water with a sound, so that you may ride them, and so that you may reflect, by their not sinking in it, despite its fluidity, its thinness and its extreme subtlety, upon the oneness of God and His power.

When He gave as the reason for the subjection the benefit of the sea itself, namely eating and what follows it, He joined to that benefit by it, saying (exalted is He): ﴿And that you may seek﴾; that is, seek with great seeking by riding it; ﴿of His bounty﴾; that is, of God's, by reaching with them the far-off lands for trade and other things; ﴿and that perhaps you will be grateful﴾ for these blessings which you would be unable to attain were it not for His subjecting it.

Al-makhr: the cutting of water to the right and left. It is also the sound of the wind when its blowing grows strong. It begins with what sinks at times and floats at others by choice, and it mentions second what by nature sinks, and third what by its nature floats.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 15:

When he mentioned the valleys that descend and govern the seas, he followed them with the firm highlands, which are like tent-pegs, as a reminder of the blessings in them. So He said: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾; that is, He placed them in it with a placing, as though He hurled them into it with a hurling; mountains, ﴿firm﴾, touching it and adorning its sides, lest it ﴿shake﴾; that is, lest it incline, quaking to the right and to the left, so that dizziness (al-maid), which afflicts the rider of the sea, would befall you ﴿with you﴾. Thus, it is steady for the sake of that casting, steady even though its roundness (al-kurriyyah) requires motion.

When he mentioned the depressions and followed them with the pegs, he went on to what rivers commonly gush forth from them, conjoining it to ﴿firm mountains﴾ because the verb ja'ala (He placed) implies its meaning. So He said: ﴿and rivers﴾. The strongest proof of the earth's stability is what preceded it, the mention of the seas, and what follows it, the discussion of the rivers. For if it moved, even by the measure of a hair's breadth each day, the seas would drown those on the side of the lowland, and the courses of the rivers would reverse, so their benefits would turn into the greatest harms. And if the seas grew by what the rivers pour into them over the passing of night and the recurrence of day, they would drown the earth. But He (exalted) arranged the matter with His wisdom in an arrangement that the thoughts of the wise cannot fully grasp: He made the heat of the sun reach the earth throughout the whole of summer and part of the other seasons, so it penetrated its depths and grew hot in its depths during winter, heating the waters of the seas and others. Vapors rose from them as steam rises from a boiling cooking pot, in proportion to what the rivers pour into them. Those vapors condensed in the atmosphere into water when they cooled, and rain descended from them, giving life to the earth after its death. Some of it seeped into its depths as God willed, and so it replenished the rivers; therefore they increase with the increase of rain and decrease with its decrease, and so it is each year. This necessitated that the sea remain in its state without increase. Glory be to the Arranger, the Wise, the Mighty, the All-Knowing.

When he mentioned that, he followed it with what leads to the benefits of each of these: so He (exalted) said: ﴿and roads﴾.

Since the mountains, seas and rivers are indications of the sensible and the spiritual paths, He (exalted) said: ﴿that you may be guided﴾; that is, guidance is achieved, so that you may be guided to your aims.

(p-128) Since the indicators on earth are not confined to one kind, He said: ﴿and landmarks﴾, i.e., from mountains and other things. The plural of ʿalāmah (sign, indicator) is a form by which meaning is known, whether through writing, speech, gesture, or appearance. It may be a conventional sign, or it may be a demonstrative proof.

Since guidance by the star is the most beneficial and most general of indications, and the clearest of them on land and sea, by night and by day, He drew attention to its greatness by shifting to the third-person absent form (iltifat, a shift in grammatical person), to convey generality, lest one think the addressee is specific and the matter does not extend beyond him. So He (exalted) said: ﴿and by the star they﴾, i.e., all the people of the earth. The most entitled to this are the first addressees, namely the Quraysh, then all the Arabs, due to their great knowledge of the stars, ﴿are guided﴾. He placed the prepositional phrase first to draw attention to the fact that the indication of others, relative to it, is lowly.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 16, verse 17:

When he had finished presenting the proofs of God's oneness (tawhid) in their most complete form, their best order, and their most eloquent arrangement, and there remained no doubt that the Creator is none other than God, given what has been established of His oneness, the perfection of His knowledge, His power, and the completeness of His wisdom, in that He made those proofs (p-129) into general blessings and complete favours, together with the clear incapacity of everything they claim to be divine apart from Him, and the clarity that He, glorified is He, is free to choose in all of His creation, because of the variation in existence and in modes between things where nothing requires variation except choice, it became established by this that He is able to bring about whatever He wills. He said, giving the cause of this: ﴿Is then He who creates﴾, that is, who renews that whenever He wills and as He wills, so His incapacity is impossible in any respect, because His partnership is possible; ﴿like one who﴾, whose partnership is possible, ﴿is the origin of that﴾, because ﴿He does not create﴾, that is, that does not come from Him at any time, from the idols and others, in their inability to bring about what He says, which entails that it would be possible and created. Had the comparison been reversed, as has been said, this estimation would not have conveyed the force of rebuke against them that it does by bringing the highest down from its rank. He used the word "one who" (man) because they named them gods, and the most they could be is rational. So when the attribute of divinity is negated from them together with the inability to do anything, it is negated without it by a fortiori reasoning.

When He had based on these proofs the denial of their making the Creator equal to others in incapacity, (p-130) He based on this denial the denial of their remembering, as an urging on them to remember in a way that results in abandoning association (shirk). So He said: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾, by what you witness of that, even in some respects, which is conveyed by idgham (assimilation of the doubled consonant in *tadhakkarun*), so that you may recall what its belief is due.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i, *Nazm al-Durar*, on Surah 16, verse 18:

Since the decreed things (*al-maqdurat*, all that God has decreed) cannot be counted, and most of them are blessings upon the servants, reminding them of their Creator, He (Exalted) said, bestowing favor upon them through His kindness without any cause on their part: ﴿And if you count﴾, i.e., all of you, ﴿the favor of God﴾, i.e., the bounty of the King, who has no lord other than Him, ﴿upon you﴾. Even if it is a single blessing, its branches exceed counting. ﴿You cannot enumerate it﴾, i.e., you cannot master its number, and your capacity does not reach it, along with its ingratitude and your complete turning away from thanking Him for it. So if you were grateful, He would increase you from His bounty.

Since they deserved the removal of blessings, by turning away from remembrance and being blind to insight, he pointed to the cause of their flowing. He (Exalted) said: ﴿Indeed God﴾, i.e., the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, with all the attributes of generosity and retribution, ﴿is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾. Therefore He pours His blessings upon you, while you are immersed in what necessitates His vengeance.

Since it is the custom that one whose kindness is denied quickly moves to cut it off upon knowing of the disbelief, it might occur to someone that the reason for the continuous flow of favours is ignorance of the ingratitude, or that ingratitude of which one is unaware does not fall under forgiveness. He said, threatening and making the pronoun explicit by the Greatest Name (on which the surah is built) to separate the Creator from others, and so that the threat is not thought to be restricted to the aspect of forgiveness, indicating that this is a consequence of what has passed: ﴿And Allah﴾; that is, the One who possesses complete encompassment of all attributes of honour and retribution; ﴿knows﴾; that is, absolutely; ﴿what you conceal﴾; that is, all of it. Since concealment may be taken to mean being alone, and so his knowledge would not indicate public display, He (exalted is He) said: ﴿and what you disclose﴾, so that the magnitude of the multiplication of the requirements of gratitude and the ugliness of disbelief may be known. As for the idols, they know nothing; there is no one more foolish than one who worships them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 20:

When He (exalted be He) established for Himself perfect power and complete knowledge, and that He alone is the Creator, He began to set forth the proofs of how far removed from divinity are those whom they associate with Him, by negating those attributes from them. So He (exalted be He) said: ﴿And those whom they call upon﴾; that is, with the call of worship; ﴿besides Allah﴾; that is, the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection; ﴿create nothing﴾. And since a claimant might assert of something that it does not create but is itself not created, He said: ﴿and they are created﴾.

(p-132) Since among created things there are the dead and the living, and the dead is the furthest thing from the attributes of God, He said — negating life from them after having negated power and knowledge (which entails that their worshippers would be nobler than they are, and which entails that by submitting to them they are in utmost folly): ﴿They are dead﴾. And since the attribute may be applied to what is not characterized by it, figuratively, on account of its not benefiting, by way of its opposite, even though it is actually present in it and deeply rooted in it, He said: ﴿not living﴾, clarifying that what is meant by this is the actual negation of life, in contrast to what God is characterized by — ﴿Surely His is the creation﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] — of being living and never dying. Perhaps He limited Himself to describing them as "dead" — although they are dead — rather than "not living," because that, along with being sufficient for the purpose of the context (which is to distance them from divinity), would be applicable to every created thing claimed to be divine, even if it possesses life, since its life is transient and followed by death; and whoever is like that is far from the attribute of divinity.

And since they — despite their knowledge that the idols are stones with no life — were being addressed from within them by the tongues of devils, as is mentioned in the biographies (siyar) and other books composed on the voices of the jinn, so that they came to think that they had knowledge in this respect; and for this reason they used to think that they harm and benefit, there was a need to negate knowledge from them. And since they were informed through their tongues of some of what they had stolen by listening (p-133) and it would happen as they had been told, He did not negate absolute knowledge from them; rather He negated what no one other than God has knowledge of, because they do not report anything about it except that its falsehood becomes evident. So He said (exalted is He), counting resurrection among what is agreed upon: ﴿And they do not perceive﴾ — i.e., in this state, as the meaning of "mā" indicates; ﴿when﴾ — i.e., at what time; ﴿they will be raised﴾. Thus He negated from them absolute perception, which is more general than knowledge, so that everything more specific than it is negated as well.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 22:

Since the proofs of resurrection have been established in their standing, their signs made clear, their beacon raised high, and their lights spread abroad, he (al-Biqa'i) pursued the discussion of them in the manner of a matter about which there is no disagreement except regarding knowledge of its time, with agreement on its basis, because it is among the necessary implications of moral obligation (taklif). And since with all this the powerlessness of their partners (shurakA'ihim) became clear, he indicated that the source of powerlessness is accepting plurality, as guidance toward the proof of mutual hindrance (burhan al-tamana'u, i.e., the argument from mutual interference). So he said, by way of resumption (isti'naf), since it is necessarily a consequence of what preceded: ﴿Your God﴾, i.e., O creatures, all of you, is the one truly worshipped; ﴿is One God﴾, i.e., characterized by divinity absolutely, in relation to every person, every time and every place; ﴿One﴾, who does not admit plurality, which is the source of deficiency, in any respect whatsoever. For plurality necessitates the possibility of mutual hindrance, which necessitates powerlessness, which necessitates distance from the rank of divinity. ﴿So as for those﴾, i.e., it follows from this that those who ﴿do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, i.e., the abode of recompense and the place where judgment is manifested, which is the fruit of sovereignty and justice, on which greatness depends; ﴿their hearts are denying﴾, i.e., ignorant that He is One, because of the hardness that they have, not because the matter is confused, as was mentioned previously in (surat) Hud, that the root n-k-r revolves around strength, and this entails firmness, so hardness results. ﴿And they﴾, i.e., while the state is that they, because of denying the Hereafter, ﴿are arrogant﴾, i.e., their characteristic is arrogance toward everything that does not agree with their desires, which is seeking elevation by refusing to accept the truth out of disdain for its people; thus they arrive at a degree at which the sun is hidden from them, as He (Most High) said: ﴿They were not able to hear, nor were they able to see﴾ [Hud: 20]. Perhaps "arrogant" indicates that "denying" (munkiratun) means: denying that of which they are in fact aware.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 23:

Since they are (for the human being is the most contentious of things in argument), they may deny arrogance and claim that if the truth had become manifest to them, they would have turned in repentance. He said, by way of a reply to one who seems to say: They do not refuse out of arrogance when they have no doubt that this is the speech of God:

﴿Without doubt﴾; that is, there is no doubt that ﴿Allah﴾; that is, the One who encompasses everything in power and knowledge; ﴿knows﴾, with knowledge of both the unseen and the witnessed, ﴿what they conceal﴾; that is, (p-135) what they hide, absolutely or in relation to some people. And since knowledge of the secret does not entail knowledge of what is openly declared, as has passed more than once, He said: ﴿and what they disclose﴾. So He reported this only concerning a matter that is certain and admits of no dispute.

And since this carries the sense of a threat, for the meaning is: He will surely requite them for the minutest and the greatest of that, without forgiving any of it, as will be stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿that they may bear their burdens in full﴾ [al-Nahl: 25], He gave the reason for this meaning with His saying: ﴿Indeed, He﴾; that is, the One who knows the secret and the open; ﴿does not love the arrogant﴾; that is, those who are arrogant toward the truth, whatever it may be.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 24:

Since disparaging the Qur'an, given the established fact of their inability to produce its like (mu'arada), was a sign of arrogance, He (Exalted is He) said, conjoining it to His saying "their hearts deny" (qulubuhum munkira): ﴿And when it is said﴾, i.e., by whatever speaker it may be, at whatever time it may be, even if it is repeated, ﴿to them﴾, i.e., to those who deny the Hereafter, ﴿"What is it that your Lord has sent down?"﴾, i.e., what thing, ﴿your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who does good to you and manages your affairs, ﴿they say﴾, being obstinate about its sending down, counting "dha" (this) as a relative pronoun (mawsula) and not as an intensifier of the interrogative: "That which you claim has been sent down, it has not been sent down. Rather, it is ﴿tales of the ancients﴾." This is despite their incapacity, after being challenged, to produce a single surah like it, and despite their knowledge that it is the most eloquent of speech, and that no word from any person, earlier or later, could be more eloquent than it, [without them saying that something is more eloquent than it].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 25:

Since the Book is the straight path (al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm) that rescues from destruction, and their saying this was an obstruction from it, it was, along with being misguidance (ḍalāl), also misleading (iḍlāl). It is known that whoever goes astray bears the sin of his own straying, and whoever misleads bears the burden (wizr) of his misleading. This is not hidden from anyone of sound intellect. Since this is clear, and since they claimed to be the most perceptive of people regarding hidden matters, how much more so regarding manifest ones, the words ﴿that they may bear﴾ are very fitting, for they know with certainty that this is necessarily binding on them, even if they say otherwise with their tongues.

Or it may be said: this was said because, although ignorance is more fitting for them than it, it is the lightest of their conditions. For they either know that by this slander they have done what is not rightfully theirs, or they do not. On the second case they are the most ignorant of people. On the first case, either they supposed that they would be held accountable for it, or they did not. On the second case, creation would be left aimless (sudan), and this has nothing to do with wisdom (ḥikmah), so whoever holds this belief is in a very great ignorance. On the first case, they witness many wrongdoers who are not recompensed in this world, and so wisdom necessitates for them the belief in the Hereafter, so that the good-doer and the evil-doer may be recompensed thereby. This is the lightest of the previously mentioned conditions. And it is not hidden what folly there is in venturing into the like of this, which contradicts their claim to be the most perceptive of people. The matter has thus come to mockery (tahakkum) of them, for they were attributed to knowledge, of which ignorance would be better.

﴿Their burdens﴾: those which they personally committed, because they turned away from the truth out of arrogance, not out of doubt.

Since God, in His bounty, expiates for the people of faith their minor sins through acts of obedience and by avoiding major sins, and since this expiation is conditional upon faith, and since these people had disbelieved by denying the Book, He said, ﴿in full﴾: none of the burden of what they concealed or what they displayed is diminished, whether by concealment, forgetfulness, expiation, or anything else, without any deficiency in any attribute. It is more emphatic than "complete" (tāmmah), because completeness may exist in number while there is a deficiency in some attribute. ﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾: the day about which there is no doubt, and from whose coming there is no escape. ﴿And﴾ [the "و" here is conjunctive]; ﴿that they may bear﴾ [the "لِيَحْمِلُوا" is joined]; ﴿from﴾ [the "مِن" is partitive], like ﴿the burdens﴾ of the ignorant weak ones ﴿whom they mislead﴾, so they go astray through them, just as those who went astray had made clear; ﴿without knowledge﴾. They bear some of their burdens without personally committing them, because they have a causal role in them, without the burdens of those who went astray through them being diminished at all, even though they were ignorant, because they have intellects which are such that they guide to asking the people of remembrance (ahl al-dhikr), and innate dispositions (fiṭar) which, at first presentation, recoil from falsehood, but they neglected these.

Then he resumed warning (tanbīh) about the great harm that results to them from what they commit, as a threat to them, and so He said: ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear.﴾ He placed the interrogative particle of denial (hamzat al-inkār) before the negating particle, so that it becomes an affirmation in the most emphatic manner.

[Commentary of al-Biqa'i, *Nazm al-Durar*, on Surah 16, verse 26]

Since the purpose of this arrogance was to obliterate the truth and conceal its matter, without openly declaring hostility, but rather by putting forward a semblance that might sometimes be accepted, even though its weakness is extreme, by minds that are weaker still, and since this is the reality of *makr* (scheming), which is covering and concealment, as he explained in *al-Ra'd* at His words (Exalted is He): ﴿Nay, the scheming of those who disbelieve has been made attractive to them﴾ [13:33], He began to threaten the schemers and warn them of what befell those who were greater than them in number and stronger in power, and to give the believers hope of victory over them, through His great might and severe retribution. So He said (Exalted is He): ﴿Those before them had already schemed﴾. And since the intended subject of the report is specific people who did not encompass the whole of earlier time, He introduced the preposition and said (Exalted is He): ﴿from before them﴾, meaning of those whose traces they saw and whose dwellings they entered. ﴿So God came at﴾, that is, with what He possesses of the totality of greatness, ﴿their building﴾, that is, the coming of might and vengeance, ﴿from the foundations﴾ upon which they had built their scheming. ﴿So it collapsed﴾, that is, it fell with a great noise because of its ruin, ﴿upon them, the roof﴾. And since the Arabs would say, "A roof collapsed on us, and a wall fell upon us" (when it belonged to them), even if it had not fallen upon them, as Abu Hayyan transmitted it from Ibn al-A'rabi, He (Exalted is He) turned away from this figurative sense to the literal sense of falling, restricted by the preposition, saying: ﴿from above them﴾. They were beneath it, so they perished, as is the nature of a building when its foundations are removed.

Since *makr* is harm in secret, because it is killing by means of a stratagem toward an objectionable end, He made clear that what befell them of punishment was of the same kind as what they had done, by His words: ﴿And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾, that is, the punishment on which the messengers agreed in threatening those who refused. ﴿From where they did not perceive﴾, because the means they had prepared for their own victory was precisely the means of their overthrow. This is by way of illustration. It was also said that it is literal regarding what Nimrod built of the tower.

**Mention of his story from the Torah:**

In the first book of it, in enumerating the sons of Noah (peace be upon him), it says: "And Cush, that is, the son of Ham son of Noah, begot Nimrod, who was the first mighty one on the earth. He was a mighty hunter before the LORD; therefore it is said, 'Like Nimrod, the mighty hunter before the LORD.'" The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Akkad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. From that land he went out to Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen, between Nineveh and Calah, which is the great city. Then, after counting the descendants of Noah (peace be upon him) and their kingdoms, it says: "These are the clans of the sons of Noah, according to their genealogies, in their nations. From these the nations spread abroad on the earth after the flood. Now the whole earth had one language and the same words. And as they migrated from the east, they came upon a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. And they said to one another, 'Come, let us make bricks and burn them thoroughly.' And they had brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar. Then they said, 'Come, let us build ourselves a city, and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.' The LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of man had built. And the LORD said, 'Behold, they are one people, and they have all one language, and this is only the beginning of what they will do. And now nothing that they propose to do will be impossible for them. Come, let us go down and there confuse their language, so that they may not understand one another's speech.' So the LORD dispersed them from there over the face of all the earth, and they left off building the city. Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. And from there the LORD dispersed them over the face of all the earth." End of quotation.

Some Jewish scholars told me that "Babel" is an Arabicized form of "Bubal," and the meaning of "Bubal" in Hebrew is "dispersion." This is what is in the Torah.

As for the exegetes (*mufassirun*), they mentioned that the tower was built in a tall form, in height and solidity, and that God (Exalted is He) destroyed it, so there was a great tremor, and because of the magnitude of its terror, the languages of the people of the earth were scattered into many modes, which none can count except their Creator. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 27:

When He, glorified and exalted, had explained the condition of the rebellious deniers who opposed Him in this world, He began to mention their condition in the Hereafter, to confirm the Hereafter and to show that their punishment is not confined to the worldly life. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾; that is, God, who did to them in this world what has preceded, will bring about a disgrace witnessed by all creatures [p. 142] standing on that Day. Thus there will befall them, as a recompense for their arrogance, a humiliation beyond description. He joined it with "then" (thumma) because of their disbelief in it and because of its terror and greatness, before which every terror seems small. ﴿And He will say﴾; that is, to them in that gathering, as a rebuke and reproach: ﴿Where are My partners﴾, according to what you used to claim? He, glorified is He, attributed them to His own sanctified self, because this is more decisive in rebuking them and more indicative of the extremity of His anger. ﴿Whom you used to﴾; that is, in a state from which you never separated: ﴿oppose [tushāqqūna] concerning them﴾, that is, My allies, so that by opposing them you stand on a side other than theirs, submitting to what does not deserve submission and being arrogant toward those from whom turning away is not fitting. [Will they then] ﴿not come to your aid or defend themselves on this Day?﴾ It was also read with a kasra on the nūn (tushāqqīna), because opposing the one commanded is the same as opposing the one who commands.

Since the situation calls for majesty and greatness, which necessarily entails increased awe, and from which the disgraced generally become mute and unable to answer, even if they had an answer; and since one of the most important purposes in punishing them is justice, through the gladdening of the allies and their gloating over them as a recompense for what they used to do to them in this world; and since gloating is the most beloved thing to the one who gloats, the greatest thing feared by the one gloated over, and the greatest consolation for the wronged; this indicates their silence, out of reluctance to hasten to answer. This is shown by delaying the predicate about it, and by placing first the predicate about the gloating of their enemies over them, in the context of an answer to one who asks: "Did the believers know of this?" It was said: ﴿Those who were given knowledge said﴾. Since knowledge is an honour to the one who possesses it absolutely, He used the passive form for His statement: ﴿who were given knowledge﴾; that is, those who benefited from it in following the path of salvation, from among the prophets, peace be upon them, and those among their nations who obeyed them. This indicates that the one who is destroyed may be deprived of knowledge, even if he is the most knowledgeable of people. He turned away from saying "their enemies," or "the believers," or similar, out of honour for them by describing them with knowledge, which is the noblest of attributes, since it is the source of every virtue; and as an allusion that what drives the disbelievers to arrogance is ignorance, which is the cause of every vice. ﴿Indeed, disgrace﴾; that is, the humiliating affliction; ﴿today﴾; that is, the Day of Decision, in which the successful one attains the sure outcome; ﴿and evil﴾; that is, everything that causes distress; ﴿is upon the disbelievers﴾; that is, those deeply immersed in disbelief, [p. 144] who were arrogant in matters that do not call for arrogance, not upon others.

Then he encouraged them toward repentance by His saying: ﴿Those whose souls the angels take﴾. It is read with the ta' above the line (*tatawaffāhum*, with a feminine verb) in the recitation of the majority (*al-Jumhūr*), because the plural noun (*jamʿ*) is feminine. It is read with the yā' below the line (*yatawaffāhum*, with a masculine verb) in the recitation of Ḥamzah, because the plural noun is not feminine. Their death occurred in two ways: a light death, indicated by the feminine form, because the disbeliever's disbelief was light; and another, a heavy and severe death, because the disbeliever's disbelief was severe. Neither of the two ta's is elided, to indicate the wretchedness of their state, since it is not possible for good to reach them at their death in disbelief. This differs from what preceded concerning the one who abandons emigration in *al-Nisāʾ* (Q. 4:97). ﴿The angels﴾, that is, those entrusted with death, while they are ﴿wrongdoers to themselves﴾, by placing themselves, through arrogance toward the Mighty King, in a place other than their proper place.

When this was complete in this wondrous manner and this lofty, impregnable style, he began the report of their answer in a way that informs of their condition, and said: ﴿Then they will offer submission﴾, that is, from themselves, right after the words of the guardians and because of the question of the Lord of Majesty; ﴿submission﴾, that is, surrender and humility, in place of that arrogance and haughtiness, saying (p-145)- committing a lie without any shame -: ﴿We were not doing any evil﴾. They went to extremes in the denial, so they said: ﴿any evil﴾. It is as if it were said: this is indeed a great calumny on that glorious day. Then what was said to them? It was said: ﴿Yes﴾, you did do the greatest evil. Then he gave the reason for refuting their denial by his saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, that is, the One who encompasses everything, ﴿is All-Knowing﴾, that is, of perfect knowledge from every aspect, ﴿of what you used to do﴾, that is, by nature and disposition, ﴿of deviation﴾ — that is, of misguidance and leading others astray. So denial is not open to you. Has the time not come for you to desist from ignorance in what harms you and does not benefit you, and what lowers you and does not raise you?!

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 29:

Since this act, together with this knowledge, was the cause of entering Hell without any weight being assigned to them, because there is no weight for what has had its foundation ruined, he said, following up and giving the cause: ﴿So enter the gates of Hell﴾; that is, O disbelievers; ﴿the gates of it﴾; that is, the gates of its levels and its depths; ﴿abiding therein﴾; that is, deeming eternity in it ﴿therein﴾; that is, in Hell, which is customarily the place of frowning upon whoever enters it.

Since this station is one of opposition, and its matter is exceedingly ugly, this entry was the ugliest of entries, and it was the cause of saying: ﴿Then wretched is﴾ (fa-la-bi'sa), with the particle that gathers all the aspects of blame, ﴿the abode of the arrogant﴾, in the manner of emphasis and of stating the attribute by which they deserved that; because of the prior lie in their saying, "We did not do any evil" (p-146), as an indirect implication that they are deserving, to the utmost degree of their dullness, of finding Hell pleasing, just as they lied despite complete knowledge that no lie passes on that Day.

And when the report about those who denied what God sent down through the angels upon the prophets, peace be upon them, "the Spirit of His command," was complete, denying their merit and arrogantly claiming what was not theirs by objecting to their Creator, He began the report about those who affirmed, confirming their guides, acknowledging their merit, and submitting to the One whose servants they are in preferring whom He wills. He thereby drew attention to the quality that obliged them to acknowledge the truth. He said, omitting ﴿idhā﴾ ("when") to indicate approval of even the least good and praise for it, even if it is not repeated: ﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God﴾; that is, who feared the punishment of God. ﴿"What"﴾; that is, what thing ﴿has your Lord sent down﴾; that is, the One who is good to you, from His Spirit, the Giver of life to spirits, upon His Messenger? ﴿They will say﴾; acknowledging the sending down, not hesitating in speech, understanding that ﴿dhā﴾ ("this") is emphatic for the interrogative and not in the sense of ﴿alladhī﴾ ("what"): ﴿Good﴾ He sent down. The readers were unanimous in putting this in the accusative and the first in the nominative, to distinguish the answer of the affirmer from that of the denier: the affirmer matches the answer to the question, while the denier turns his answer away from the question (p. 147). Then He began to encourage them with the good outcome that is theirs, in the form of an answer to a question as if someone had said: "What do they get for that?" So it was said, placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, as praise for them and to generalize to whoever shares their quality: ﴿For those who did good﴾. He thus showed that their acknowledgment of this is a good deed. Then He reported about it by His saying: ﴿In this world is good﴾; that is, a reward for them for their good deeds. ﴿Is the reward for good anything but good?﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 60].

Since this abode is swiftly passing, He reported their state in the Hereafter, saying: ﴿And the home of the Hereafter is better﴾; that is, as reward and final destination. Then He praised it and praised them by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing﴾; that is, it is so. This encourages the quality that was the cause of their attaining it, which is fear, contrary to the arrogance with which He described the wicked. It is by the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, and by omitting the object of praise because what indicates it precedes it, and it is suitable for the estimate of "the world," that is, for those who worked in it with piety, and for the estimate of "the Hereafter," which is clear.

Since this praise was meant to whet the appetite for a detailed account of it, He said: ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾; that is, a dwelling in which there is no departure; ﴿they will enter them﴾, the state in which they will be; ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾; that is, beneath their mansions; ﴿the rivers﴾. Then he answered one who seemed to ask about the fruits and other things in them, with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿For them therein﴾; that is, exclusively; not in anything other than them; ﴿is whatever they wish﴾, without it being brought to them from anywhere else. Then He increased the encouragement with His saying: ﴿Thus﴾; that is, like this great reward; ﴿Allah repays﴾; that is, the One who possesses all perfection; ﴿those who are mindful of Him﴾; that is, those firmly established in the attribute of taqwa (God-consciousness, piety).

Then he urged adherence to taqwa (God-consciousness) by alerting that what matters is the state at death. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are pure﴾; that is, they take their souls complete, lacking nothing of the spirit or of its meanings, as is indicated by the affirmation of the two taʾs and the clear articulation (of the verb). ﴿Pure﴾; that is, purified from wronging themselves through disbelief, adorned with the adornment of faith. It is as if it were said: What do the angels say to them? So it was said: ﴿They say﴾; that is, repeating for emphasis, to calm what they were created upon of reverence for the majesty of God through taqwa: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾. And it is said to them, to confirm their triumph: ﴿Enter the Garden﴾; that is, the abode of delight, which has no like; ﴿for what you used to do﴾; that is, by nature and disposition; ﴿you did﴾, as an encouragement to them toward the deeds which they could not perform except by the mercy of God toward them, by His granting them success in them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 33:

(p-149) When (may He be exalted) had informed about the states of the disbelievers, who asked about the descent of the angels, after He had weakened their doubts, and informed about the taking of souls by the angels for them and for their opposites, the believers, indicating by this that His custom is that they (the angels) do not descend except to bring down the Spirit by His command, upon whomever He singles out for that, or for a decisive matter with no delay in it, He said, rebuking them: ﴿Do they await﴾; that is, these disbelievers, in their slackness in confirming the messengers regarding what their Lord has sent down; and He stripped the verb (of a subject marker) to indicate the nearness of what they are awaiting: ﴿except that there come to them﴾; that is, by the command of Allah; ﴿the angels﴾; and they do not come to them except with the like of what came to those before them, from among the wrongdoers whose matter We have recounted, if they do not repent; ﴿or there come the command of your Lord﴾; that is, the One who is good to you, who manages your affair; with a command that decides the dispute without an intermediary angel or other than him.

Since this is a frightening matter, it necessarily leads one who has understanding to ask: Has anyone other than these done this? It is said: Yes; ﴿Thus﴾; that is, the like of this act, far removed, because of its ugliness, from the methods of the intelligent, of plotting in arranging harm and of belief and speech; (p-150) ﴿did those who﴾ (came) before them; and since the doers were like their deeds in denial, the time was not fully encompassed, so the preposition was introduced, and He (exalted) said: ﴿from before them.
