And Allah did not wrong them﴾; that is, while the truth is that Allah did not wrong them; He, to whom belongs all perfection, in His decree of that upon them; because He is the absolutely free disposer, and the King who is not questioned about what He does; ﴿but they were﴾; that is, by nature and disposition; ﴿wronging themselves﴾; that is, exclusively; ﴿so they deserved punishment﴾, because the proof was established against them, according to the custom by which your habits proceed, regarding one who engages in evil without being compelled to it by an apparent compulsion; and this very thing is the reason for the sending of the messengers, the establishing of the laws and the creeds.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 34:**

﴿So there befell them﴾, that is: as a consequence of their wronging themselves, the evil ﴿consequences﴾, that is, the punishments, or the recompense, ﴿of what they had done﴾ befell them, and ﴿encompassed﴾, that is, surrounded them with a comprehensive encompassing, ﴿them﴾, with the punishment, and with what was sent with it of the angels. ﴿That which they used to mock﴾, that is, specifically, out of arrogance toward accepting the truth.

The root *ḥāqa* (حاق), with its six permutations, *ḥ-w-q*, *ḥ-q-w*, *q-ḥ-w*, *q-w-ḥ*, *w-q-ḥ*, and *ḥ-y-q* (of the weak-waw and weak-ya' types), revolves around the notion of encompassing. It entails the hardness of the encompassing thing and the softness of the thing encompassed. From it: *ḥāqa bihi al-shay'* ("the thing befell him"), meaning it descended upon him and encompassed him. *Al-ḥayq* (الحيق) is what envelops a person of the disagreeable thing he has done (p. 151). *Ḥāqa fīhi al-sayf* ("the sword worked in it") means it cut, that is, it acted; this is naming by the part, since in its action death, which encompasses the appointed term, usually occurs. *Ḥāqa bihim al-amr* means the matter clung to them, became binding upon them, and descended upon them. *Al-ḥay'qa* is a tree like wormwood with which dates are eaten, as if it encompasses the date. *Ḥāyaqahu* means he envied him and hated him, because of that encompassing.

*Al-ḥūq*, with a *ḍamma*, is what surrounds the glans of the penis from its edges. With both *ḍamma* and *fatḥa* together, it means roundness in the penis. *Al-ḥawq*, with a *fatḥa* only, means encompassing. *Al-aḥwaq* and *al-muḥawwaq*, on the pattern of *mu'aẓẓam*, mean the glans, as if it is specific to that because of its largeness. From it comes *fayshala ḥawqā'* ("a great mass"), meaning great, as if because of its greatness it is the one whose edge appears rather than others. *Arḍ maḥūqa*, with a *ḍamma* on the *ḥā'*, means land with little vegetation because of little rain, as if it resembles the glans in its smoothness. *Turikat al-nakhla ḥawqā'* means the palm was left burnt around its base, when fire is kindled among its stumps, because of the circling of the fire around it, or because after the palm fronds burn it resembles the penis or its head. *Al-ḥawqa*, with a *fatḥa*, means a group of deceivers, because a group has the strength of circling. If *al-mumakhraq* is from lying, then whoever persists in it has crookedness. If it is from *al-mikhraq*, which is the handkerchief wrapped for play, then playing with it takes the form of circling. *Ḥawqa 'alayhi, taḥwīqan* means he twisted speech against him. *Al-ḥawq*, also with a *fatḥa*, means sweeping, rubbing, and smoothing, because each of these returns the hand to near its place, so it resembles encompassing, even if by bending.

*Al-ḥaqw* is the flank, which is what lies between the head of the hip bone and the rib, the lower part, because it is the place where the waistcloth encompasses. The waistcloth itself is called *ḥaqw*, because it is its instrument. Or *al-ḥaqw* is the place where the waistcloth is tied. *Al-ḥaqw* is also a thick place, raised above the flood, from hardness and roundness, because the flood encompasses it or nearly does. *Min al-sahm* means the place of the feathers, because it resembles the *ḥaqw* in its roundness, the thickness of some parts, the thinness of others, and the encompassing of the feathers around it. *Min al-thaniyya* means its two sides, from encompassing, or from general crookedness. *Al-ḥaqwa* is a pain in the abdomen from eating meat, because its pain reaches the *ḥaqw*. *Al-uqḥuwān* is a plant whose flower is arranged in a circle. *Aqāḥī al-amr* are its first signs, because these usually encompass it. *Qaḥā al-māl* means he took the wealth, because of the encompassing that it entails. *Al-miqḥāh* is the shovel, because it encompasses what is shoveled.

From softness: *qāḥa al-jurḥ, yaqūḥ* means the wound became filled with pure pus not mixed with blood, like *qāḥa, yaqīḥ*, of the weak-waw and weak-ya' types, and usually because of the roundness that it entails. *Qawaḥa al-jurḥ* means the wound swelled up, either from the thick elevated place above the flood, or from its roundness. *Qāḥa al-bayt* means he swept the house, like *qawaḥahu*. *Al-qāḥa* is the courtyard, usually because of its roundness. *Aqāḥa* means he insisted on refusal after being asked, either from removal, that is, he removed the softness, or from hardness.

From hardness: *al-wuqāḥ* is for the hard hoof, and it too is from roundness. *Rajul wuqāḥ al-wajh* means a man of little shame, from it. *Al-muwaqqaḥ*, on the pattern of *mu'aẓẓam*, means the one who has been tested. *Tawqīḥ al-ḥawḍ* means repairing it with clay and flat stones, for roundness and hardness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 35:

When what was strange about their speech and their outcome, in their evil condition, was complete, and he concluded with their threat, he linked it to His saying, "And when it is said to them, 'What has your Lord sent down?'" as another cause for the threat, marveling at their state in this matter. So He said: ﴿And those who associated partners [with Allah] said﴾; that is, the firmly rooted among them in this description, and those who follow them, by way of objection to those who call them to tawhid (monotheism), whether a prophet or others, arguing by divine decree out of obstinacy, and objecting to the One who is not questioned about what He does, [claiming] that because of His power over everything (p-154) He does not need to send messengers, so sending them is pointless. Exalted is Allah, the Wise, above their saying. This is the saying of one who seeks the reason behind His rulings (exalted is He) and His acts. It is a false saying, because He, glorified is He, is the one who does what He wills, whether or not He makes His wisdom known to the servants: ﴿If Allah had willed﴾; that is, the Supreme King, encompassing everything in power and knowledge, [had willed] our not worshipping other than Him: ﴿we would not have worshipped﴾. Since all ranks fall short of His rank, and they vary, and what they worship of idols is of the lowest rank, they introduced the preposition and said: ﴿besides Him﴾; and they went to the extreme in negation, saying: ﴿anything﴾; that is, of things: ﴿neither we nor our fathers﴾ before us. Since they mentioned the root, they followed it with the branch, saying: ﴿nor would we have forbidden﴾; that is, upon ourselves, ﴿besides Him﴾; that is, besides His command, ﴿anything﴾; because what He wills does not fail, according to your claim. But He did not will non-existence, so He willed the existence of what we are upon. So we follow what He willed and do not deviate from it, because He wills only what is true. The wretched, by this word of theirs, which is truth that they intended as falsehood, have strayed from the point that the basis of happiness and wretchedness is only conformity with the command, not conformity with the will. So whatever act or abstention accords with the command, its doer is made happy, and whatever opposes it, the proof is established against its doer, (p-155) according to the customs of people, and he becomes wretched.

When the veil of this deceptive saying was torn away, and it was as if it were said, finding it far-fetched: "Did others say it?" It was answered: "Yes." ﴿Likewise﴾; that is, like this far-fetched saying, which lacks rectitude and guidance, namely objecting to their Lord regarding the sending of messengers, barring the permissibility of sending by this weak doubt. For He (exalted is He) wills the manifestation of the fruit of sovereignty through judgment, according to what servants understand of establishing proof through voluntary acts, even if they are by His decree, because that is hidden from the servants. ﴿Did﴾; that is, denied, by the evidence of the favor; ﴿those who﴾, and it indicates the absence of totality of time by His saying: ﴿before them﴾. It was a denial, because their saying implied that what they were upon is something Allah is pleased with, while the messengers say that He is not pleased with it, and He is not pleased except with what those who practice it have been informed will be rewarded or will not be punished. So this became a reason for denouncing them with His saying: ﴿So is there﴾; that is, then what is there; ﴿upon the messengers﴾; that is, those who in reality have no messengers other than them, and they are those whom Allah sent to call the servants, one generation after another; and since the interrogation (p-156) carries the meaning of negation, as previously mentioned, but it was framed in its form so that it would be like asserting a matter with its proof, He said: ﴿except the clear conveyance﴾. They have indeed conveyed to you and made clear to you, so the burden of disobedience has become yours alone.

[p. 157] Since the sending of messengers implies their distribution among the nations, this was a point where one would expect an explicit statement of that. So He said, to dispel the distress of this anticipation, to negate the arrival of any such possibility, to indicate that this earlier statement is aimed primarily at their objection to sending (the messengers), to console His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and to urge them to take heed. This is a continuation of what is implied as follows: "We certainly sent you to this your nation, so that they would worship Allah alone and avoid the taghut (false objects of worship). Among them are those whom We guided, and among them are those upon whom error was decreed. Without doubt, some of them were pleasing to Allah and some were displeasing to Him, for the ruling on two opposites is never the same." He said: ﴿And certainly We sent into every nation a messenger﴾. That is, by Allah, We certainly sent, by virtue of the majesty that We possess, whoever opposes which is seized. ﴿Into every nation﴾ among the nations that came before you. ﴿A messenger﴾. So no one remained on earth to whom the call had not reached. And because messengers may sometimes come from outside the people they are sent to, such as Lot and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, to the Companions of the Thicket, and Sulayman, peace be upon him, to others than the Children of Israel, and to all others among the people of the earth reached by his rule, He did not restrict it with "from among them." Since sending implies the meaning of saying, the sense is: they went to them saying: ﴿Worship Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿alone﴾; ﴿and avoid﴾, that is, with all your effort, ﴿the taghut﴾, as Our messenger has commanded you. ﴿Among them﴾, that is: the sending of messengers resulted in the nations being of two kinds: among them were those ﴿whom Allah guided﴾, that is, He who has complete comprehension of the truth, so guidance was due to them. They saw the truth and acted upon it by following the guiding callers in what they were commanded by Allah. So Paradise was due to them. ﴿And among them were those upon whom error was decreed﴾, that is, it became firmly established in the utmost degree, ﴿upon him﴾, by Allah causing him to go astray. So he rejected the command and did not act upon it, and acted in accordance with the requirement of the will. For a command may not be what is willed, while the will must be what is willed, and what agrees with the will may be a doer of error, so its punishment was decreed upon him, and the Fire was due to him, and he perished, because no proof remained for him with which to defend himself. Had everything He willed been true, both groups would have been correct, and neither would have been punished. But this is not the case. Rather, He punished the disobedient and saved the obedient in every nation, according to what the messengers had said. This is the meaning of Allah's pleasure, using the name of the cause for its effect (metonymy). Thus this definitively indicates the truthfulness of the messengers and the falsehood of their opponents. So the verse is of the type of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which something is mentioned on one side and omitted from the other, and vice versa): it mentioned the act of guidance first, as evidence for the act of misguidance second, and mentioned the decreeing of error second, as evidence for the decreeing of guidance first.

Then He turned to address them, indicating that after this definitive proof, in the view of insight, nothing remains except the proof perceptible to sight. So He said: ﴿So travel﴾, that is: if you, the addressees, are in doubt about the report of the messengers, then travel ﴿through the earth﴾, that is, its kind; ﴿and observe﴾, that is, when you travel and pass by the abodes of the deniers and their traces. Here He used the particle "fa" (then/so), which indicates immediacy without delay, because the situation calls for reasoning that rescues from error, and it is obligatory to hasten to abandon it, unlike "thumma unzuru" (then look) in al-An'am, due to what has preceded. He used the interrogative to indicate that their conditions are something that must be asked about, for the sake of taking warning from it. So He said: ﴿How was the end﴾, that is, a state from which there is no ability to escape, ﴿of those who denied﴾, that is, the final outcome of ʿAd and those after them, whose reports you have received from those whom you followed in disbelief among your forefathers. For they denied the messengers in what I commanded them to convey, opposing My command and acting according to My will. So I brought destruction upon them, because they opposed My command by their own choice, while being ignorant of My will. Thus the proof was established against them, according to what people commonly recognize among themselves.

Since it was established in the argument that, after the conveying of proof up to a perceptible matter, nothing remains but obstinacy, he turned away from them, addressing instead the one who is compassionate toward them and kind to them. He said, consoling him (may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace (ﷺ)): ﴿If you are eager for their guidance﴾, so that you seek it with the utmost of your effort and striving, ﴿then indeed Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿does not guide﴾, that is, He does not, by creating guidance in the heart. This is according to the reading of the Kufans, with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the dal. And (there is no guide for them) "in any way whatsoever," according to the reading of the majority, in the passive voice: ﴿whom He causes to go astray﴾, that is, whom He judges to be astray, and He is the One who led them astray, so no one else can guide them, because no one can overcome His command. It was also read irregularly (shadhdhan) with a fatha on the ya', from "ḍalla" in the sense of "nasiya" (to forget). Then the meaning is: the guidance of one whom He has forgotten is not possible, that is, one whom He has left out of guidance, as one leaves what is forgotten, because nothing is in the hand of anyone else. Al-Saghani reported in Majma' al-Bahrayn that one says, "ḍalla fulān al-ba'ir," meaning "adallahu" (he caused the camel to go astray). And ḍalāl (going astray), according to the Arabs, is taking a path other than the straight way of intent. So the meaning is that he was the cause of the camel taking a course other than the intended one. Thus the meaning of the verse is: He does not guide whom Allah causes to go astray (with a fatha on the ya'), that is, he becomes the cause of his taking a course other than the straight way. So do not grieve, and do not let your chest be constricted over their not being affected by your counsel and your sincerity in calling them. Let it not enter your mind that there is any deficiency in your supplication; the deficiency lies only in their blind mirrors (of perception). Upon you is nothing but conveying (the message). His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And they have no﴾, that is, these people whom Allah has led astray, and all whom He leads astray, ﴿helpers﴾, that is, who will help them at the time of their being recompensed for going astray, to rescue them from the calamity that befalls them because of it, as was done with the deniers before them. It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the consequence of what precedes it, which is: "there is no guide for them," since Allah did not intend their going astray. It is also a rebuke, a reproach, an incitement, and a stirring to make them stand up on their own and seek help from whomever they wish in establishing proof for what they claim, that they are the people most following the truth: either by demonstrating the soundness of their belief, or by helping them to turn back from it when they are unable to do so, or by warding off the punishment from them when it descends upon them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 38:

(p-161) Since it was their due, after the proofs had been established of His complete power, the all-encompassing scope of His knowledge, and the far-reaching reach of His wisdom in originating all created things, those we know and those we do not know, in the most wondrous arrangement and the finest order, that they should confirm the guides (hudah) in their announcement that He, glory be to Him, will return them for resurrection (ba'th); yet they did not do so, nor did they entertain any possibility of it, but instead swore to deny it without any doubt having presented itself to them, and without any report of knowledge having reached them, acting like the coarse, heedless, stupid, and rebellious boor. God, glory be to Him, followed this with another expression of wonder at their condition, saying, joining it by conjunction (ʿatfan) to "And those who associated partners said" — because each of the two sentences serves to explain their denial of the messengers and the wonder at them in that, and it indicates that their belief in the content of this sentence is what emboldened them to say the first one and what branches from it:

﴿And they swore by God﴾; that is, the Greatest King; ﴿with their most emphatic oaths﴾; the oaths were described as "jahd" (emphatic) because of how much they exaggerated in them; ﴿God will not raise up one who dies﴾; that is, He who has comprehensive encompassing of everything; ﴿will not raise up anyone who dies﴾; that is, He will not bring back to life anyone after his death; relying on mere deeming it unlikely, on their part, that which custom itself had not brought about among them; rigidly refusing to loosen it by [considering] that the first creation was also without custom; together with their claim that they are the most intelligent of people, the sharpest of minds, and the keenest of understandings.

Then He refuted them with His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Yes indeed﴾; that is, He will certainly raise them up; for there is no obstacle to Him in that (p-162) — and He has promised it as ﴿a promise﴾; and He made clear that it is necessary, by His saying: ﴿upon Him﴾; and He added emphasis to it, in opposition to their striving in their oaths, by His saying: ﴿truly﴾; that is, because He is capable of it; and He does not change His word; so its occurrence became obligatory in wisdom; and the matter of resurrection is known to every intelligent person who hears the words of the guides, leaving aside his own desires; ﴿but most of the people﴾; that is, with what they have of confusion; ﴿do not know﴾; that is, they have no knowledge that would bring them to it, because it is of the unseen realm; their minds cannot reach it without guidance from God; nor do they accept the words of those who call to Him, whom He strengthened with a spirit from Himself; because they are confined to what their minds lead them to, and those are limited to the realm of the witnessed; they cannot ascend from it to the realm of the unseen without an intermediary from Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He; therefore you see the man among them refusing that, deeming it unlikely that something rational should exist which does not reach him by mere reason alone; and he is a manifest adversary.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 16, verse 39:

When he had made clear that this (resurrection) must necessarily come to pass, because the promise of it had already been given by the All-Powerful, he explained its wisdom with a clear matter, namely that it is not permissible to abandon it in any way. That matter is this: no sound mind can accept that anyone, whether a king or someone lower than a king, commands his servants to do something and then neglects them, not questioning them about it, especially if their disagreement leads to boycott and fighting. (p-163) How much more so if he is a ruler! How much more so if he is wise! How much more so when he is the most judicious of judges! So he said, linking it to what the word "Bala" (Yes indeed) indicates: ﴿That He may make clear to them﴾, i.e., He has done it and promised it, so He will raise them up that He may make clear to them ﴿that about which they differ﴾, i.e., about which their disagreement exists ﴿therein﴾, from the resurrection and other matters; and He will recompense each soul according to what it has done, because that is part of justice, which is His act. ﴿And that those who disbelieved may know﴾, i.e., they were ignorant of the signs that point to it, so it is as if they had concealed them, since by their clarity they cannot be unknown; ﴿that they were﴾, i.e., by nature and disposition, ﴿liars﴾, i.e., deeply immersed in lying, in their denial of the return and their claim that they alone are the ones who attain success; (they will know) with the knowledge of certainty, the eye of certainty, and the truth of certainty.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 40:

When He had explained its inevitability and its wisdom, He explained its possibility, its ease for Him, and its lightness in His sight. So He (may He be exalted) said: ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing﴾; that is, by what We possess of greatness; ﴿when We intend it﴾ for bringing into existence and for restoring it; ﴿is only that We say to it﴾; that is, We intend its coming into being. Then he mentioned the reported form of the inner speech, saying, building from "kāna" (the complete, non-defective verb, meaning "to come into being" rather than a copula), that which indicates the compliance of things intended with the compliance of the one commanded to the one commanding and obeyed: ﴿"Be!"﴾; that is, come into existence; ﴿and it is﴾; that is, the saying results in its existing, at the moment the power is directed at it, without any delay at all. So We created creation in order that We might command them and forbid them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 41:

Since the intended sense (taqdir), as a detailing of the two groups mentioned earlier and an encouragement to emigration (hijrah), because it comes after faith as the most firm of the bonds of Islam, is: "As for those who disbelieved (p-164) and were deceived by what they witnessed of the fleeting worldly goods, We will surely humiliate them in this world and the Hereafter, and We will surely requite them for all that they used to do," the following is joined to it: ﴿And those who emigrated﴾, i.e., they carried out emigration (muhajarah), fleeing with their religion. So they abandoned their fathers, their sons, their relatives among the disbelievers, their homelands, and everything they were forbidden to keep; ﴿for the sake of Allah﴾, i.e., the Supreme King who possesses the attributes of perfection, after those who denied the Resurrection persisted in harming them, so they left them their lands.

Since their emigration did not extend over a long period of separation, because some of those they had left died and others embraced Islam, after they had endured their wrongdoing for as long as Allah willed, He said (Exalted is He): ﴿after they had been wronged﴾, i.e., their wrongdoing was inflicted by the disbelievers. It was phrased in the passive because what is to be feared is the occurrence of wrongdoing, not that it comes from a specific person. ﴿We will surely settle them﴾, i.e., We will bring into being for them a dwelling-place worthy of being returned to, by means of what We possess of angels and other hosts and all grandeur; ﴿in this world﴾ as an abode; ﴿good﴾, i.e., great, magnificent, as a reward for them for their service to Us, by exalting their affair, even though the polytheists dislike it, as one who reflects will see, by My protecting My friends despite their small number. The matter will be revealed soon, in a disclosure (p-165) that no one will be ignorant of. Thus the verse is evidence for what precedes it.

Since the intended sense is: "And We will surely settle them in the Hereafter with a great reward," the following is joined to it: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter﴾, which is prepared for them, ﴿is greater﴾ than what I have given them in this world; ﴿if only they knew﴾, i.e., if the disbelievers had knowledge by their natures, by having an intellect with which they would reflect, they would know, through My goodness to My friends in this world, from My protection of them against their enemies in their obstinacy despite their numbers and their small number, and My bestowing of My favours upon them, especially in the lands to which they emigrated, such as Abyssinia, Madinah and others, despite their exertion to prevent these favours from reaching them, that I gather for My friends both abodes, and that My goodness to them in the Hereafter is greater. It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say, whenever he gave a share to a man among the emigrants: "Take it; may Allah bless it for you. This is what Allah promised you in this world, and what He has stored up for you in the Hereafter is greater and more excellent." Then he recited this verse.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 42:

When He had alerted them to His beneficence toward them, and there was at the outset a kind of obscurity in this (matter), because the unbelievers appeared (to be prospering) at first sight, He described them with what is needed for completing the enticement, as an urging and an inflaming (of their zeal). So He (Exalted is He) said, describing the emigrants, as an explanation of the root of what moved them (p-166) to what made them deserving of this great reward: ﴿Those who endured patiently﴾; that is, they practised patience toward what befell them of hardships from the disbelievers and others, in remaining among them for a period, and then in emigrating, by leaving the homeland, which is the sanctuary of Allah, whose love is instilled in every heart. How much more so for the hearts of those for whom it is the place where their heads first fell (their birthplace), and the familiar abode of their bodies and souls. (They endured patiently) also in giving up their lives in jihad and other than that. He turned the speech to the description of beneficence, as an alert to what moves one to trust (in Allah). So He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾; that is, upon the One who does good to them by bringing them into existence and guiding them, alone; ﴿they put their trust﴾ in every state they desire, being content with the decree of Allah (Exalted is He).

When (Exalted is He) informed that He had sent the Messengers, and that the outcome for those who denied them was destruction, as shown by the traces they left behind, and since they had discredited the message on two grounds, that the Messenger is a human being, and that no angel accompanies him to support him, He refuted this by saying, addressing the noblest of His creation (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family), because he was the one best able to make them understand him, and he is the greatest of those who relied upon Allah and endured patiently. He referred to the Name of Majesty (al-Jalal), to clarify that He manifests whom He wills over whom He wwills: ﴿And We did not send﴾, meaning, by the greatness that is Ours. Since the sending in actuality occurred only in some periods of time, He indicated this with the prepositional phrase (p-167), so He said: ﴿before you﴾, to the nations among the various groups of mankind; ﴿except men﴾, not angels, but human beings, who were in the utmost capacity for reliance upon Allah and patience, which is the seat of manliness (al-rijlah): ﴿to whom We revealed﴾, through the mediation of the angels. How excellent is the connection of this to "for the patient"! For the Messengers are the most patient of people.

Since they had resorted to asking the People of the Book about some matters, and since they had been given knowledge from Allah, He made the command to ask them about this information a consequence of this report, so He said, addressing them and everyone else who wished to verify, from among others: ﴿So ask﴾, meaning, O you who deny, and whoever else wishes, ﴿the people of the Reminder﴾, meaning, those with knowledge of the Book. It was called "reminder" (dhikr) because remembrance, which is the opposite of forgetfulness, stands in the position of the cause that leads to it, so the term is applied to it, as if the ignorant person were forgetful, even though he is not forgetful. Likewise, the Reminder, which is the spoken discourse that is mentioned, is a cause of knowledge.

Since they had some awareness of this through hearing reports of the nations before them, He pointed to it with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿If you do not know﴾, meaning, by natural disposition and inclination. Or it is a rebuke against being content with ignorance.

When the messengers of kings were accompanied by something that made their truthfulness known, [al-Biqa'i] said, in answer to one who seems to ask, "By what evidence were they sent?": ﴿with the clear proofs﴾, which make their truthfulness known; ﴿and the scriptures﴾, meaning the books that guide to the commands of the one who sent them. (p-168)

Since the Qur'an is the greatest of the proofs, he indicated this by mentioning it, while implying the other miracles. He used the conjunctive waw and said, joining it to what is implied, "And thus We sent you with the manifest miracles": ﴿And We have sent down﴾, that is, by the greatness We possess; ﴿to you﴾, that is, while you are the most honoured of creation; ﴿the Reminder﴾, that is, the Book that brings about remembrance, that raises rank, and that leads to the stations of nobility; ﴿so that you may explain to the people﴾, all of them, by what Allah has given you of understanding, in which you surpass all creation, and of eloquence, which is the greatest and most eloquent of tongues. Allah has brought you in this to a rank that no one else has reached. ﴿What has been sent down﴾, that is, what has been revealed, ﴿to them﴾, of this sacred law (shar') that guides to the happiness of both abodes, by clarifying what is general (mujmal) and explaining what is obscure, from the science of the foundations of religion (usul al-din), whose head is monotheism (tawhid), and from resurrection (ba'th) and other matters. It also includes making clear to the people of earlier scriptures what their books contained, so that it may show them what was abrogated (nusikha, naskh) and what they altered and were thereby transformed (famusikha).

Since the implied sense is, "So that, through the excellence of your exposition, they may act," he joined to it, as an explanation of the nobility of knowledge (p-169), His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and that they may reflect﴾, that is, when they consider its exquisite styles and its lofty, refined meanings, they will, through reflection upon it, by means of the doors of exposition that I have opened for them, arrive at the states of the angels, so that their spirits overcome their bodies. Then they will know that He, exalted is He, is One, Capable, and an Agent by choice, and that He will raise people for recompense. Thus they will obey Him out of desire and fear, and they will combine the two honours: the obedience to which spirits summon, and the restraint from disobedience to which souls, through the bodies, are inclined.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 45:

When He (subhanahu) drew attention to reflection, and reflection calls the intelligent person to accept what is possible and to keep far from danger, He consequently denounced feeling secure against that. So He (exalted is He) said: ﴿Do those who devise evil schemes feel secure﴾; that is, have they reflected so that they repent, or do they persist in their insolence? Do ﴿those who devised the evil schemes﴾, by plotting to kill the prophets and to extinguish the light of God with which He sent them, feel secure ﴿that God will not cause the earth to swallow them up﴾, that they will not be repaid in kind for their deeds, by God ﴿causing the earth to swallow them﴾; that is, God who encompasses everything; ﴿them﴾, that is, specifically; ﴿the earth﴾, so that they find themselves within it, unable to turn about in any way, neither by resisting nor otherwise, as was done to Qarun and his companions, and to the people of Lut (peace be upon him) before them; ﴿or that the punishment will not come upon them﴾ in a different state; ﴿from where they do not perceive﴾ it in either of these two states, having no awareness of it at all, while they are in a state of tranquility and ease, in sleep or heedlessness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 46:

﴿Or He seizes them﴾ (p-170); that is, God seizes them with His punishment ﴿while they are going about﴾, that is, in the midst of their movements and their dealings, while their senses are present and their faculties gathered.

Since these three states were assumed to be states of their feeling secure from punishment, and since feeling secure from an enemy arises from the belief that he has no power over them, He explained this with His words (Exalted is He): ﴿So they cannot escape Him﴾; that is, in any of these states, whether they are heedless or alert, it is all the same to Us.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 16, verse 47:

He did not give a reason for what follows with that, because one who is apprehensive (mutakhawwif) allows for the possibility of incapacity. So He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Or He seizes them﴾; that is, Allah seizes them in wrath; ﴿while they are in fear﴾; that is, apprehensive of the punishment; and guarding against what befell those before them of the punishment of annihilation (al-isti'sal). It is also possible that what is meant by what has passed is the punishment of annihilation, and that by this seizing is meant gradual seizing, for al-takhawwuf (apprehension) means diminution (al-tanaqquss) according to the Hudhayl tribe. It is narrated that ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, asked the people about it, and they were silent. Then an old man from the Hudhayl answered him that it means diminution (al-tanaqquss). ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Do the Arabs know that in their poetry?" He said: "Yes. Our poet Abu Kabir al-Hudhali said, describing a she-camel:"

*Takhawwafa al-rahlu minha tamikan qaradan* ∗∗∗ *kama takhawwafa ʿudda al-nabʿati al-safanu*

ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O people, keep to your diwan, so that you do not go astray." They said: "And what is our diwan?" He said: "The poetry of the Jahiliyyah, for in it is the tafsir (exegesis) of your Book and the meanings of your speech."

Since the implied sense is: "They did not feel secure about that in reality," but their ignorance of Allah—because of the length of His forbearance and His clemency—deceived them, He made what follows a consequence of this, turning to direct address to win their sympathy: ﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾; that is, the One who is good to you by destroying whom He wills and sparing whom He wills; ﴿is Most Kind﴾ (ra'uf); that is, of perfect compassion toward whoever seeks access to Him by some means, and likewise toward whoever turns away from Him in the most complete turning away. He alluded to this with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Merciful﴾ (rahim); that is, from His granting them respite in their disbelief and transgression, while having power over them, arises the knowledge that His leaving off hastening their punishment is nothing but out of His tenderness and mercy.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 48:

When He instilled fear in them, He pointed to the completeness of His power over that and over other things, by His saying, linking it to what is implied (its estimated meaning being: "Have they not seen their inability to achieve what they desire, and His compelling them to what they do not desire, so that by this they might know His power and their own weakness, and so that they might know that His pardoning their crimes is a benefaction from Him toward them and a kindness to them?"): ﴿Have they not﴾. And since their due was to hasten to repentance, and they did not do so, He turned away from them as a warning. In the reading of the majority, He said (exalted is He): ﴿see﴾, with the yā’ (third person). Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read it with the second person, in keeping with what precedes it; that is, let them look with the eyes of sight while reflecting with the insight of the heart. He made clear their distance from the divine knowledge by the particle of limit (ilā, "to"), and so He said (exalted is He): ﴿at what God has created﴾; that is, the One to whom belongs all command; ﴿of any thing﴾; that is, which has a shadow; ﴿that casts its shadows﴾; that is, the shadows return toward the direction of the object casting them; ﴿its shadow﴾, which is what the object casting it screens from the sun, extending beyond it; ﴿to the right﴾, which is the area on the right of one who turns toward the north, facing the south, which is the direction of the Ka‘bah for those in the lands of Shām, the dwelling place of the prophets (peace be upon them). The singular is used because the shadow is first formed, as the sun rises, straight toward that direction, evenly; and the plural is used in His saying ﴿and the left﴾, because whenever the sun rises higher, that shadow turns back toward the direction behind the object casting it, and it continues so until, at sunset, it stands toward its left, in the opposite of what it had stood toward at sunrise. Since after its standing toward the right, it seeks in its shifting the direction of the left, those directions in which it shifts are named after what it seeks, as an alert to this. In this there is an indication of the scarcity of what is right and straight, and the abundance of what is deviant and inferior.

Since a large number of those who submit indicates more strongly the subjugation and is more awe-inspiring, He used the plural, in view of the meaning of ”mā“, in His saying ﴿prostrating﴾; that is, while they are humbled ﴿to God﴾; that is, the Supreme King, with what they have of need for their Manager.

Since the extension of the shadow is compelled and no one can detach himself from it, He said, combining with the masculine plural ending (wāw and nūn) by way of predominance: ﴿and they are abased﴾, in humiliation and lowliness, none of them able to resist His disposing of him. He singled out the shadow for mention because of the swiftness of its change, and change indicates the one who changes it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 49:

When he (Allah) had judged the shadows in terms of what encompasses their owners of inanimate things and animals, and animals are more noble than inanimate things, he elevated the judgment to them specifically, so He (Exalted) said: ﴿To Allah prostrates﴾; i.e., He to whom all command belongs; ﴿prostrates﴾; i.e., submits in obedience, yielding to the decrees and running under the decrees. He expressed it with what is apparent regarding non-rational beings, along with its inclusion of rational beings, so He (Exalted) said: ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾; and since the context called for emphasis in establishing the judgment for both the obedient and the disobedient, He repeated the relative pronoun, so He (Exalted) said: ﴿and whatever is in the earth﴾; then He clarified that by His saying (Exalted): ﴿of creature﴾; i.e., rational and non-rational.

And since the one who is brought near may sometimes look down on those who draw near to him, he said, explaining the submission of those brought near and singling them out, although the speech had already included them: ﴿and the angels﴾.

And since the one who submits may be judged by his submission even if his inner state opposes his outward state, he said, indicating that among others there are those who are arrogant, so that their yielding to the will is unwilling; and he expressed the two prostrations, the one agreeing with the command and the will willingly, and the one agreeing with the will but opposing the command unwillingly, with a single word, because it is permissible to combine the two meanings of a homonym (mushtarak), and the literal and the metaphorical, in one word: ﴿while they are not arrogant﴾; i.e., the angels; ﴿they do not wax proud﴾.

Then he gave the reason for their submission with His words, as an indication that they are like others in standing between fear and hope: ﴿They fear their Lord﴾; that is, the One who brought them into being, who manages their affairs, who does good to them; a fear that comes from above them ﴿from above them﴾, an indication of the loftiness of the fear over them and its dominance over them; or, the state of their Lord, together with His goodness to them, is that He possesses loftiness and majesty, so He is the One to be feared and revered. (p-175) So they refrain from what they have been forbidden; ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾; that is, with a great motive, out of knowledge of what is due to their Lord, with no rival from self-interest, desire, or anything else. And His words (Exalted is He) ﴿they do what they are commanded﴾ indicate that they are under obligation. So they hope for His mercy toward them. The verse is of the type called ihtibak (mutual omission): the mention of fear first implies hope second, and the mention of action second implies refraining first.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 51:

Since *tawhid* (affirming God's oneness) is the greatest of the commanded matters, and disobedience in it is the greatest disobedience, and since He, glorified is He, had greatly warned against disobeying in it, He carried the matter to its end by informing that the angels fear Him. The angels are among the greatest of those who affirm God's oneness, just as they are among the greatest of those who prostrate, from among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earths. These verses are among the greatest proofs of *tawhid*, so He followed them, by way of *'atf* (conjunction) with ﴿And He has sent down to you the Reminder﴾ [An-Nahl 44], so that the proofs of reason (*'aql*) and transmission (*naql*, i.e. revealed textual evidence) would combine in support of this, and to lead (the listener) by means of the states of the angels. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Allah said﴾. For the sake of magnifying the station, He used the Most Great Name, the particular one upon which the surah is built: ﴿Do not take﴾, meaning: do not burden your original, sound natures, which are innately disposed to know that God is one, until you take in your belief ﴿two gods﴾. It is also possible that it is conjoined with what has been known from the premises mentioned at the beginning of the surah, up to His saying: ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾ [An-Nahl 21], as part of the conclusion, which is: ﴿Your God is one God﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 108], lest a contentious person say: "He did not command us with that," even if the proofs indicate it. It is also possible, and this is closer, that it is conjoined with His saying: ﴿And those who associated partners said﴾ [An-Nahl 35], as a rebuke to them, for they argued by His decree and did not hasten to comply with His command.

Since the intended meaning from the dual form had been understood, and a contentious person might say that what is forbidden is multiplying names, He said, emphasizing and affirming: ﴿two﴾, to indicate that divinity (*uluhiyyah*), because it is a locus for the possibility of rivalry, which entails incapacity, which contradicts that rank, does not accept any number at all, which negates the lofty summit. In this there is also, along with the fact that the objects of their worship were many, an indication that what is called gods, even if their number increases, in reality reduces to two: a creator and a created. It is known to every person of intellect that the created is not fit for divinity, so the matter is confined to the Creator. And if the Creator is not in it, it would necessarily be divided, and the least that can be divided is into two. The verb *ittakhadha* (to take), when its object is indefinite, is satisfied with one, as you say: "I took a house" and "I took a wife" and the like. Then He gave the reason for that prohibition by what the context required of oneness, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He is﴾, meaning: the god understood from the word "two gods", to whom this pronoun cannot be applied, other than figuratively, for it is not applied in a true sense except to what they found from His essence: ﴿God﴾, meaning: deserving this attribute absolutely.

Since the context implied oneness from the prohibition of duality, and a contentious person might have pressed that the intended meaning is affirming a god that indicates a genus, He said, removing every doubt: ﴿one﴾, meaning: it is not possible for Him to be doubled in any way, nor to be divided, because of His absolute independence from everything, and the need of everything for Him. So be among those who prostrate to Him willingly, and do not be among those who prostrate to Him only unwillingly.

Since the style of the third person does not specify the God who is speaking, He turned to the style of the first person and said, exalted is He: ﴿So Me﴾, meaning: that one is I, alone, with no partner for Me. Whoever does not affirm My oneness, I will inflict upon him, by My power, what he cannot bear, because of his weakness. Since oneness is something no intelligent person can fail to know, and it is fixed in every natural disposition, as evidenced by the agitation during trials, hardships and tribulations, and since reverence (*rahbah*), as already passed from al-Haralli (Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali) in *Al-Baqarah*, is specifically fear of what the disobedient person opposes knowledge in, He expressed it by saying, exalted is He: ﴿so fear Me﴾, singling this out: do not fear anything other than Me, whether an idol or anything else, for none of these has any power, and even if one were to entrust it with power, it would not be able to carry out that power. So the entire matter is to Me alone.

[p. 178] Since the form of address in the third person (al-ghaybah, the shift from direct address to speaking about someone absent), when used instead of the second person, indicates a mind veiled by pride, which announces the severity of seizing and the swiftness of retribution and the remoteness of rank, He returned to the direct form, and so He said (Exalted is He): ﴿And to Him belongs﴾. Thus He returned the pronoun to Allah, the proper name (al-ism al-'alam), which encompasses all the Most Beautiful Names (al-asma' al-husna): ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾. And since the matter had been affirmed and firmly established, and its intended meaning had become utterly clear, there was no need to emphasize it by repeating the negation. So He said (Exalted is He): ﴿and the earth﴾, meaning: of what you worship and of other than it. How, then, could it be conceived that any of that is a god, when it is His possession, while it is in need of time, place and other such things? ﴿And to Him is the religion﴾, meaning: submission and humility from everything that is in them and everyone who is in them, by choice and by compulsion, through the execution of decree and destiny: by health and sickness, wealth and poverty, life and death, bringing into existence and annihilation, abasement and exaltation, favour and turning away, as he explained a little earlier. To Him also belongs the requital (al-dayyunah) by recompense. ﴿Perpetual﴾, meaning: lasting, enduring, universal, unlike kings whose dominions end along with their specific limits, and objects of worship whose worship ceases at some time, [p. 179] becoming worthless after having been profitable, however long the span, and limited to certain people without others; and no day passes for any king other than Him without affairs proceeding contrary to his will, however great his authority, however lofty his rank, and however numerous his helpers. How, then, could anyone with the slightest insight conceive that other than Him is a god? The proof of this has already been given in His words: ﴿Indeed my Lord is upon a straight path﴾ [Hud: 56] in Surah Hud, and what was said there is useful to recall here.

Since this proof has been established for this attribute, and since among the concepts of religion is recompense, which regards the deeds that protect from harm, there follows from it a severe denunciation of whoever turns, in any of his deeds, toward other than Him, after knowing that He is everlasting and does not cease, and that everything else is perishable. So He said, expressing it through God-consciousness (taqwa), which is the result of awe: ﴿Is it other than Allah that you fear﴾, meaning: He to whom all greatness belongs?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 53:

And He followed that with what makes the denunciation of them a grave matter. Thus He said, clarifying that fear and hope should attach to none but Him: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾; that is, whatever has come upon you, O people, all of you, believers and disbelievers alike, ﴿of blessing﴾; that is, great or small. ﴿Then it is from Allah﴾; that is, the One encompassing everything, alone, not from anyone else.

Since their sincere devotion to Him, along with their claim that others share in divinity, was a matter of improbability, He expressed it with the particle of delay and distance in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when harm touches you﴾; that is, the slightest touch (p-180) ﴿of harm﴾ by the loss of a blessing He had bestowed upon you, ﴿then to Him﴾; that is, to Him alone, ﴿you cry out﴾; that is, you raise your voices in seeking help, because of what He placed in your sound, original natures: that there is no refuge and no escape from Him except by turning to Him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 54:

Since returning to polytheism (shirk) after sincere devotion (ikhlas) is also deemed unlikely, given their disapproval of the speed of such a transformation (istihalah), He (Exalted) says: ﴿Then when He removes﴾ — glorified is He above what you associate with Him — ﴿the harm﴾, that is, the affliction that touched you, ﴿from you﴾. And He draws attention to the swiftness with which man hastens into ingratitude (kufran), so He (Exalted) says: ﴿behold, a party﴾, that is, a group who are people of division (firqah) and misguidance (dalal), ﴿among you﴾, O servants, ﴿ascribe partners﴾ to ﴿their Lord﴾, who alone bestows favours upon them, ﴿they ascribe partners﴾, that is, they commit shirk with Him by worshipping another, changing from what they were upon when they called upon Him for help in hardship. Thus there applies to them what they have struck as a proverb concerning their dislike of it, in their saying:

Whenever a disagreeable matter occurs, it is Yad'a for her (I'll be called upon for it),
And when the hays (a mixture of dates, butter and curds) is being stirred, Jundub is called (to help).

And this is the height of ignorance.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 55:

When this was entailed by denial of the blessing, and it is the way of the intelligent and discerning person (p-181) in matters, as they claim for themselves, to overlook something of the necessary consequences of what he undertakes, He said: ﴿So that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾; that is, they bring about the concealing of the proofs of tawhid (divine unity), which the instincts of their minds guided them to; ﴿in what We have given them﴾; that is, of the blessing. This is to alert that they did not embark upon that polytheism except for this purpose, placing them in the position of the intelligent and discerning, who claim that they are the highest of them, and lifting them above the states of one who embarks upon what he does not know the outcome of. And there is no greater disgrace than this, because it yields that madness is better than an intellect whose outcome is this. So it is of the genre of mockery (tahakkum). ﴿So enjoy yourselves﴾; that is, as a result of this, He turns toward this group with the turning of one who knows and is able over them, saying: Enjoy yourselves. ﴿For soon﴾; that is, your enjoyment in this state is a cause for it to be said to you, as a threat: soon ﴿you will know﴾, after your enjoyment. So this is the turning of wrath and the threat of a bad end. And the omission of that with which they are threatened is more eloquent and more terrifying, since the soul goes off in every direction in specifying it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 56:

When He threatened them for their associating partners with Him, which entails ingratitude for the blessing, He followed it with another wonder concerning their affair. So He said, linking it to His (exalted) saying: ﴿And they swore by Allah with the utmost of their oaths﴾ [al-Nahl: 38]: (p-182) ﴿And they assign﴾, i.e., by way of repetition; ﴿to what they do not know﴾, of what they worship of idols and other things, because it is within the realm of non-existence in itself, and pure non-existence by what they ascribe to it, as He (exalted) said: ﴿Or will you inform Him of what He does not know?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33]; ﴿a share of what We have provided them﴾, by what We possess of greatness, from the tilth and the cattle and other things, drawing near to them, as its explanation has already passed in "al-An'am." You may also link it, and this is closer, to "they associate" (yushrikūn), so that it falls within the scope of ʾidhā (ﺇذا, "when"), i.e., they were suddenly confronted with associating partners in return for His blessing in delivering them, and with drawing near, through His provision, to that about which ignorance is better than knowledge, because it is non-existence, since it has no power and no benefit in the station in which they placed it. Then He turned to them with an iltifāt (a shift from third person to second person address) signifying what is deserved for this act of anger. So He said (exalted): ﴿By Allah﴾, i.e., the Most Great King; ﴿you will surely be questioned﴾ on the Day of Gathering; ﴿concerning what you used to﴾, i.e., a state which is in your natures; ﴿invent﴾, i.e., what you deliberately fabricated in this world of falsehood; a questioning of rebuke, which is the kind for which its addressee has no answer except with what discloses his disgrace.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 57:

When he had explained their foolishness in diverting what He had given them to that which is among the ranks of non-existence, which is not known, he then explained to them a folly greater than that, by their assigning to the Owner of dominion and its King the most contemptible of what they themselves esteem, of what He had brought into being for them, because of their neediness toward Him and His independence of it, in the manner of begetting, which is impossible for Him, while they themselves dislike it. Thus that became the most wondrous of wonders. So He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And they assign to Allah﴾; that is, the One about whom there is no true knowledge other than Him, since He combines the attributes of majesty and generosity.

Since the intent was to rebuke them, and femininity was sometimes applied to the noblest of trees, He specified the intended meaning by His saying: ﴿daughters﴾. So there is no more wondrous thing than them, in that they assign existence to the non-existent and unknown, and assign non-existence to the existent and known. Then He declared Himself far above that, marveling at its occurrence from a rational being, by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Glory be to Him﴾.

When He mentioned what they assigned to Him, together with absolute independence, He explained what they attributed to themselves, together with the necessity of need and weakness. So He said: ﴿And for themselves is what they desire﴾, namely of sons; and this is in a nominal sentence whose indication is permanence, so that it proclaims their disgrace, for they do not remain for their children, and their children do not remain for them, and they may even be their worst enemies.

Then He explained their condition when some of what they attributed to Him (glory be to Him) befell them. So He said (may He be exalted): ﴿And when﴾, that is, when they attribute such things; and the situation is that when ﴿one of them is given good news﴾, and since the matter is determined and the thing feared has passed, He combined the two baseness: just as He explained at the end of "as-Saffat" (al-Saffat). So He said (may He be exalted): ﴿of a female﴾, that is, he meets this good news (p-184), which deserves joy, with the birth of a soul that could be a cause for increasing this kind (and may be the cause of its happiness), indicating the greatness of God, in the opposite of what it deserves, with something that benefits him nothing, by which ﴿his face becomes dark﴾. He expressed the frowning, the displeasure, and the dust-like gloom by what boils within him of rage, in His saying (may He be exalted): ﴿black﴾, that is, from grief and aversion. Perhaps the word "became" (ẓalla) was chosen, whose meaning is working during the day, even though the intended meaning is generality during the day and otherwise, indicating the fame of this attribute, like the fame of what is witnessed during the day. ﴿And he is "kaẓīm"﴾, filled with rage at the woman, though she is in no way at fault. And "bishārah" (good news), in the original linguistic usage, is the report that changes the complexion (bashara) due to sorrow or joy; then in common linguistic usage it was specialized to joy, and it is not used except for the first kind of report. Perhaps He expressed it with this word to alert to their reversing of matters, in their attribution, their joy, their sorrow, and other of their affairs.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 59:

Since the blackening of the face and the suppression of anger (kazm) may not be accompanied by disgrace, he connected to it His (exalted) saying: ﴿He hides himself﴾, that is, he conceals himself, by placing himself in a place as if it were behind (him), so that no one has sight of him, ﴿from the people﴾, that is, the men, among whom he is, ﴿because of the evil of that whereof he was given good tidings﴾, since he counts it as disgrace. Then he explained what befalls him of bewilderment in thought at that moment by His (exalted) saying: ﴿Shall he keep it despite contempt?﴾, that is, despite humiliation and the lowering of his status. Since they used to bury the female infant (al-mawudah) in the earth in a manner other than the form of burial, He expressed it by (the word) "dass" (concealing), so He said (exalted is He): ﴿Or bury it in the dust?﴾ Ibn Maylaq said: The exegetes said: When a woman felt the pangs of labour, she would dig a small pit and sit on its edge. If she gave birth to a male, she would display him, and joy would appear among her family; but if she gave birth to a female, she would ask permission of her husband (mustawliduha). If he wished, he would keep her in contempt; and if he wished, he would order her to be thrown into the pit and the dust to be returned over her while she was alive, so that she would die. End of quotation. They said: The burying of infant daughters was practised among Mudar, Khuza'ah and Tamim.

Since their judgment this was extremely ugly, He described it with what it deserves, saying, emphasizing its ugliness: ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾, that is, by assigning to their Lord what they dislike, the One from whom they have no blessing except from Him, and assigning to themselves what they choose for themselves exclusively.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 60:

Since the explanation of this is that they spoke falsehood concerning His side (exalted is He) and their own side, He clarified what the truth is in this station. So He said (exalted is He), as an answer for one who seems to have asked: "What is to be said about that?", using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, to draw attention to the attribute that impelled them to engage in falsehoods without fear: (p-186) ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the likeness of evil﴾; that is, they do not bring faith into existence at all; ﴿the likeness of evil﴾, that is, the description of the evil: from weakness, need, humiliation, and foolishness; ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest likeness﴾; that is, He to whom belongs all perfection; ﴿the likeness﴾, that is, the description, or the measure, or the attribute, or the analogy; ﴿the highest﴾, in respect of wealth, power, and all attributes of perfection, such that no need, no weakness, and no trace of deficiency whatsoever reaches Him; and the most fitting expression for this is: "There is no god but Allah." The interpretation of the likeness in its literal sense is possible, as will be made clear, God willing, in Surah "al-Rum."

Since His affair (glorified and exalted is He) is greater than what minds perceive and what understandings reach, He indicated this by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, not other than Him; ﴿the All-Wise﴾, the One from whom nothing is withheld, so there is no equal to Him; ﴿the All-Wise﴾, who places nothing except in its proper place; so were He to deal with them according to what they deserve for these great sins that preceded from them, He would have emptied the earth of them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 61:

﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task﴾; that is, the Supreme King, who possesses the attributes of perfection; ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾, all of them. Since the context concerns wisdom, and since wrongdoing (ẓulm), which is placing a thing in other than its proper place, is highly incompatible with it, and since shirk (associating partners with Allah), whose context this is, is the greatest of wrongdoing (aẓlam al-ẓulm), he said, expressing it by a descriptive term that encompasses what has actually occurred from them and what they harbour within themselves, and which is a description of them though they have not yet actually committed it, he said: ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾; that is, He deals with them as one who looks at his adversary, dealing with him in pure justice, without regard for grace. He expressed it with the form of mufā'ala (reciprocal/contending form), because its indication of contention is more emphatic. ﴿He would not leave﴾; and since the situation required mention of wrongdoing, and since the context of this verse is harsher than the context of "Fāṭir," he expressed it by what includes every creature carried by the earth, whether on its back or in its belly, whether submerged in water or not. So he said (exalted is He): ﴿upon it﴾; that is, upon the earth, which is known to be their dwelling place, indicated by the word "dust," and he intensified the negation; so he said (exalted is He): ﴿any creature﴾; that is, any soul that crawls upon the face of the earth, because all of them are either wrongdoers who are punished for their wrongdoing, or are among the interests of the wrongdoer, so He destroys it as a punishment to the wrongdoer; or because He did not create them except for the sake of mankind, so when He destroys them, He destroys them, as occurred something close to this in the time of Noah (peace be upon him). ﴿But﴾; He does not do that to them; rather ﴿He defers them﴾ out of respite, by His wisdom and His forbearance; ﴿until a specified term﴾; which He appointed for them from eternity.

Since He has cut off knowledge of the end from what will occur, He made the announcement of what will happen therein a consequence of that, so He said: ﴿So when their term comes﴾; which He decreed for seizing them at it; ﴿they will not delay﴾; that is, from it; ﴿an hour﴾; that is, a time that is commonly understood among you. Then He conjoined to the conditional clause, from its beginning, His saying (exalted is He): ﴿nor will they advance﴾; that is, from the term, by anything.

When what preceded was a sign of their dislike of what they attributed to God (exalted is He), He followed it with explicit statement after allusion, saying (exalted is He): ﴿And they assign to God﴾; that is, while He is the Supreme King, ﴿what they dislike﴾; that is, for themselves: daughters, wealth, and partners in leadership; and [they assign to Him] what belittles their messengers and their armies, and neglect of their messages. Then He described their boldness despite this, which occurs in a place of fear, and which requires a lack of the necessary reflection that comes from lacking intellect. So He said: ﴿And their tongues describe﴾; that is, they say, believing with their speech the purity [of what they say]. Since it was a statement with no reality to it in any way, He attributed it to the tongue, saying: ﴿their tongues﴾; that is, despite this, even though it is a statement that no rational person should imagine, ﴿the lie﴾. Then He clarified it with His saying: ﴿that for them is the best﴾; that is, with Him. There is no greater ignorance, nor any worse judgment, than to be certain that the one for whom you assign what you dislike will assign to you what you love. It is as if it was said: "What then is their (p-189) position with Him?" So it was said: ﴿Without doubt﴾; that is, without any supposition or hesitation, ﴿that for them is the Fire﴾, which is the recompense of the wrongdoers; ﴿and that they will be ﴿mufratun﴾﴾; that is, made to go forward, hastened toward it, by the one who drives them ahead and hastens them. Al-Rummani said: left behind therein, from the saying of the Arabs: "I did not leave anyone behind me (ma afraṭtu warā'ī aḥadan)"; that is, I did not leave behind or abandon anyone. Nafi' recited it with the lightened form and the kasra, meaning: those who exceed in extravagance and boldness against God.

In the Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 63:

When He had made clear their final outcome, and they used to say, "Surely they will have intercessors on their behalf," He explained to them what their condition would be, by way of comparison with their like, as a threat and as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ). So He said (may He be exalted): ﴿By Allah﴾; that is, the King, the Most High. ﴿Indeed We sent﴾; that is, with the greatness that is Ours; ﴿messengers﴾ ﴿to nations﴾ of those who passed away; and since the sending had actually occurred, it did not extend over the whole span of the past, so He said: ﴿before you﴾, just as We sent you to these people. ﴿But Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾; that is, the one burning with wrath, the one cast out by the curse; ﴿their deeds﴾, just as he made these people's deeds seem fair to them, so they went astray as these went astray; ﴿so We destroyed them﴾. ﴿He is﴾, not any other, ﴿their protector today﴾, after their destruction, while they are in the Fire; and He has no power to help them. ﴿And theirs is a painful punishment﴾. So they have no protector; for had He been able to help them, He would not have delivered them to destruction, when they had obeyed Him. Rather, had they been deprived of His protection, that would have been better for them. Thus this is a denial that they have any protector, in the most emphatic manner.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 64:

(p-190) Since the sum of what has preceded is disagreement, misguidance and retribution, it is as if it were said: "So make [the truth] clear to them, and warn them, so that they may return; for We have not sent you except for that purpose." ﴿And We have not sent down to you the Book﴾; that is, with what We possess of greatness, from the direction of height; ﴿to you the Book﴾; that is, the one comprising every guidance. Since it is in the context of exhortation and exposition, He expressed it with what necessitates obligation, and said: ﴿except that you may make clear﴾; that is, with complete clarity; ﴿to them﴾; that is, to those to whom you have been sent, and they are all of creation; ﴿that about which they differ﴾; in all matters, religious and worldly; because you are the most abundant of them in knowledge and the most penetrating of them in understanding. He coordinated with the position of "li-tubayyina" (that you may make clear) what is the act of the One who sent it down, so He said (exalted is He): ﴿and as guidance﴾; that is, as a healing exposition; ﴿and mercy﴾; that is, and as honour with love.

Since that might include them, while they remain in their misguidance, He negated it by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿for a people who believe﴾. And tabyin (making clear) is a meaning that leads to knowledge of a thing distinct from other things; it may be about the meaning itself, and it may be about its soundness; and proof (burhan) is only about its soundness, so it is more specific. And ikhtilaf (disagreement) is each party going off in a direction other than that of its companion; and guidance (huda) is the making clear of the path of knowledge that leads to the truth.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 65:

(p-191) When the proof had concluded that their hearts were denying out of arrogance, along with what is connected to it, and he concluded it with what He revives hearts by means of faith and knowledge after their death through disbelief and ignorance; and since the greatest aim of the Qur'an was to establish four foundations: the divine matters (al-Ilahiyyat, theology); prophethood (al-Nubuwwat); the return (al-Ma'ad, the afterlife); and the affirmation of divine decree and predestination (al-Qada' wa'l-Qadar) and of action by choice (al-Fi'l bil-Ikhtiyar); and since the most sublime of these aims is the divine matters, he began with proofs of the Oneness (al-Wahdaniyyah), of power, and of action by choice, which entails the power to resurrect, in a manner not previously mentioned, so that it may be known that the proofs of this are more numerous than the leaves of trees and clearer than the light of day. Thus he linked, upon His saying ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ [al-Nahl: 19], His saying, bringing together in the proof the upper world and the lower world: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One to whom all command belongs, ﴿sends down from the sky﴾ at the time He wills, ﴿water﴾, by rain, snow and hail, ﴿and then revives thereby the earth﴾, the barren land. And since His custom in this was constant, and since the context was for establishing the pillars of the religion, and since the revival by water still has its effect visible in crops or trees in some lands, he removed the adverb from the preposition, because the meaning with it is more eloquent, and so He said: ﴿after its death﴾, by dryness, barrenness, and the complete crumbling of vegetation at its root and top.

And since what He established as proof for this in this surah had reached a degree at which the intelligent listener needs nothing more than hearing, (p-192) He said (Exalted is He): ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who listen﴾, that is, in the effective water, through His management, this great effect. ﴿A sign for a people who listen﴾: this alert in this style, which includes what has passed of comparison, so that they know that He sends down from His command what He wills, and by it He revives the bodies of the servants after their death, just as He revived the bodies of plants by water after their death, and the spirits of the forms by knowledge after their death. The summary is that these proofs, along with the senses, do not require much action by the heart beyond submission to the truth and abandoning stubbornness and ignorance; so it is from hearing with the ear and what arises from it of response, using the thing in its literal and figurative sense. Perhaps He did not conclude it with "they see" (yubsiroon), lest it be thought that this is from insight, and so it be thought that it requires much thought in it, and what is intended of indicating the intensity of clarity would be lost.

﴿And indeed for you﴾, i.e., O you who are addressed, immersed in blessings, ﴿in the livestock﴾. Since proofs are the means by which one crosses over from ignorance to knowledge, He said: ﴿there is a lesson﴾. It is as if it was asked: what is it? So it was said: ﴿We give you to drink﴾, with a *ḍamma* (short vowel u) on the nūn, according to the reading of the majority, from *asqāhu* (أسقاه), when one prepares for someone what he drinks constantly, whether from a river, or milk, or other things. And with a *fatḥa* (short vowel a) in the reading of Nāfi', Ibn 'Āmir, and 'Āṣim, in the transmission of Shu'ba, from *saqāhu* (سقاه), when one hands someone something and he drinks it.

Since *al-an'ām* (الأنعام) is a collective noun (*ism jam'*), it was treated as singular, as Sībawayh transmitted. The thing given to drink is mentioned, which is milk, because the context of the surah, which enumerates blessings, requires it. Thus the intended meaning was clearly the females, and the ambiguity was removed despite the masculine pronoun. He said: ﴿of what﴾, i.e., of some of that which, ﴿is in their bellies﴾. So He used the masculine pronoun (*dhakkara al-ḍamīr*) because there is no confusion, and to indicate the strength of the meaning, since this is the surah of blessings, unlike what occurs in *al-Mu'minūn*.

Since the place of the lesson is the separation of milk from other things, He placed first His saying: ﴿from between excrement﴾, which is the residue that descends into the rumen (*al-kirsh*, الكرش), and when it leaves it, it is no longer called *farth* (فرث); ﴿and blood﴾, ﴿pure milk﴾, free from any mixture of the two or of other things, that does not carry any taint of color or smell. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: when the animal eats fodder and it settles in its rumen, it cooks it, so its lowest part becomes excrement, its middle part becomes milk, and its uppermost part becomes blood. The liver is set over these three kinds, dividing them, so the blood flows in the veins, the milk in the udder, and the excrement remains in the rumen. ﴿Palatable﴾, i.e., easy to pass down the throat, ﴿for those who drink﴾.

Then he linked to it (ʿaṭafa ʿalayhi) something more precious than it in their estimation and closer to it in the meanings mentioned. So He (Exalted is He) said, linking it to "We give you to drink" (nusqīkum):

﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes﴾. Since they have a role in making what is mentioned from it, unlike milk, for which they have no craft at all, He attributed the matter to them. This is an indication of the disliking of intoxication (sukr), and a preparation for the prohibition of it in His words, beginning a new clause: ﴿you take﴾ (tattakhidhūna), i.e., by your own making and effort. For the sake of beginning this new clause, it was necessary to have His words ﴿from it﴾, i.e., from its juice. He expressed intoxication (sukr) by the verbal noun (maṣdar) for the sake of conveying its ugliness, and He increased the conveying by using the heavier of the two verbal nouns, which is the one with the vowel on the middle letter. It is said: "sakara sukran wa sakaran," like "rashada rushdan wa rashadan" and "naḥala naḥlan wa naḥalan." So He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿sakaran﴾, i.e., possessing intoxication, intoxicating, exciting, blocking the channels of the intellect, ugly, not agreeable as a provision; ﴿and a good provision﴾, which does not result in harm to body or intellect, such as vinegar, date syrup, and others, and which does not block any of the channels, but rather may open them, like lawful good things, for it illuminates the heart and widens the intellect, and all condiments open the blockages of the body. This is like His (Exalted is He) bestowing upon you the intellect, than which there is nothing better; a people used it correctly in monotheism, while others reversed it and defiled it with polytheism.

Al-Rummānī said: It was said: "sakar" is what is forbidden of drinks, and "good provision" is what is permitted of them — from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ibrāhīm, al-Shaʿbī, Abū Razīn, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Qatādah (may Allah be pleased with them all).

"Sakar" in the language has four meanings: the first: what intoxicates; the second: what is fed of food; the third: stillness (sukūn); the fourth: the verbal noun from "sakara," whose origin is the blocking of channels by what is thrown into them; from it comes "al-sikr" (with a kasra, then a sukūn), meaning a dam. Whoever takes "sakar" to mean intoxication says: it has been abrogated by the verse of al-Mā'idah. Expressing it by what conveys the blocking of channels conveys its disliking at the time when it was lawful.

The verse is of ihtibāk (the rhetorical device of mutual implication): mention of "sakar" first indicates "opening" second, and mention of "ḥasan" (good) indicates "qabīḥ" (ugly) first. So this verse is the most evident in the Qur'an for the Mu'tazilah in that provision (rizq) is applied to what is unlawful.

Because the two verses of al-Anʿām and al-Naḥl (the cattle and the trees) are close to each other, He (Exalted is He) joined them, saying: ﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., in this great matter of these benefits, ﴿is a sign﴾. And because the matter of both is clear in demonstrating the perfect power of the Creator and His oneness, He said: ﴿for a people who reason﴾.

When the matter of the bee (*nahl*) served to demonstrate the completeness of power and the perfection of wisdom, it was more wondrous than what preceded it and more precious. He mentioned it three times and placed it last, because it is the least of the three in their estimation.
