He said, using the form (ifti'al) to indicate that this is not done except through severe struggle against the self, because the sound natural disposition (fitrah) strongly recoils from it: ﴿And do not make your oaths a means of deception (dakhal) among yourselves﴾; that is, corruption, treachery, sickness, and deceit. ﴿Among you﴾; that is, within the depths of your minds and your bodies. ﴿Lest a foot slip﴾; that is, so that this becomes a cause for a foot to slip ﴿after it was firmly planted﴾; a foot that is at the height of greatness because of its firmness, ﴿after its being established﴾ in its place of stability in which it was, whether in religion or in worldly affairs, so that it no longer has a place to rest and falls from its rank. The slipping of a foot is a figure of speech the Arabs use for anyone who falls into ruin after having been safe. ﴿And you would taste evil﴾ along with that slip; ﴿because you hindered﴾ yourselves, and hindered others, by your oaths, with which you intended corruption, to conceal the truth, ﴿from the way of Allah﴾; that is, the Supreme King. This action will keep recurring for you as long as you remain in this condition. ﴿And for you﴾, in addition to that, ﴿is a great punishment﴾, established and inseparable, if you die upon that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 95:

When this was specific to oaths, he followed it with the prohibition of treachery in the general sense of covenant, as a reinforcement upon reinforcement, to indicate the gravity of breaking it. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿And do not exchange﴾; that is, do not burden yourselves with obstinacy and with neglecting to consider the consequences by taking and substituting ﴿the covenant of Allah﴾; that is, the One to whom all perfection belongs; ﴿for a small price﴾; that is, from the trifles of this world, even if you see it as much. Then he gave the reason for its smallness by His saying (Exalted): ﴿What is with Allah﴾; that is, the One to whom majesty and honour belong, of the reward of both abodes; ﴿is better for you﴾; and none turns away from the good to what is lesser except an obstinate person deficient in intellect. Then he conditioned knowing its excellence upon their being among those of knowledge, saying (Exalted): ﴿if you know﴾; that is, by your natural dispositions; ﴿know﴾; that is, among those whose knowledge is renewed, and that you are not counted among the cattle. Thus the covenant, which encompasses oaths, began in these verses with the command to fulfil it and was concluded with the prohibition against breaking it; and oaths, which are more specific than it, stand midway between the command and the prohibition related to it. Thus the exhortation to them reached a degree of great emphasis and a rank of lofty affirmation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 96:

Then he explained its excellence and its abundance by His saying (exalted is He), by way of causal explanation: ﴿What is with you﴾, i.e., of the transient goods of this world, which is what you pursue by your natures, ﴿will run out﴾, i.e., will perish. So its possessor's life is troubled, to the utmost degree of his delight in its cessation, or in his anticipating its cessation, if he is among those who know. ﴿But what is with God﴾, i.e., that over which He has all command, of reward, ﴿is lasting.﴾ So He will surely give you from it if you remain steadfast in His covenant. Then he hinted at the hardship involved in this, by way of coordination with this implied condition, and so He said (exalted is He), emphasizing it to refute the deniers: ﴿And We will surely reward﴾, i.e., "Allah" according to the reading of the majority, with the letter ya', and "We" according to the reading of Ibn Kathir and 'Asim, with the letter nun, a shift to the first person plural for glorification. ﴿Those who were patient﴾ in fulfilling what pleases Him of commands and prohibitions. ﴿Their reward﴾. And since generous kings pay rewards in accordance with the deeds, from the best and what is less than it, He informed that He aims at the best and raises everything to it, and equates the lesser with it. So He said: ﴿according to the best of what they used to do﴾, i.e., the state that is their innate disposition. ﴿They used to do.﴾

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 97:

When He had promised, after He had threatened, He followed it with what makes clear that this does not pertain to the noble alone or the lowly alone; rather it revolves with the attribute He had alluded to earlier: with justice at one time, and with covenant at another, and that is faith. So He (Exalted is He) said, as an answer to one who might have said, "This is specific to one person and not another," encouraging the generality of the sacred laws of Islam: ﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾. And since it is general, and it might have seemed to be restricted to males, He clarified the intended scope of its generality by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿whether male or female﴾. So He generalized, then restricted, pointing with the singular to the scarcity of those firmly rooted (in knowledge), by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿while he is a believer﴾. (p-249)

Since a person, the higher he rises in the degrees of faith, the more he is liable to trials and tests, He (Exalted is He) made clear that this does not contradict his happiness. For this reason He emphasized His saying: ﴿We will surely cause him to live﴾, to repel what those who are led on gradually (al-mustadrijun) might imagine, by what He hastens to them of their good things in the worldly life. ﴿A good life﴾, that is, in this world, through what We give him of firmness of foot and purity of disposition. ﴿And We will surely reward them﴾, all of them, ﴿their reward﴾, in this world and the Hereafter, ﴿according to the best of what they used to do﴾, that is, the innate state (kawnan jibbiyyan) of their doing. The scholars (may Allah be pleased with them) said: The obedient one is in a pleasant living; if he is wealthy, there is no discussion about it; and if he is poor, then through contentment and satisfaction, by the judgment of the tranquil soul. The wicked one is the opposite: if he is poor, it is obvious; and if he is wealthy, his greed does not leave him to enjoy it, so he is always in a straitened living.

When these rulings were established on these sublime aspects, and their excellent wording and noble context pointed to purposes that, despite their majesty, are obscure and subtle, it became clear that the Qur'an is "an exposition of everything" (﴿and an exposition of all things﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]) for whoever is safe from the perils of desire and the snares of Satan. He concluded this by urging righteous deeds. The Qur'an, through recitation, reflection, and acting upon what it contains, is among the most excellent righteous deeds. Because of this, it was stated that when this Qur'an, revealed in such superior styles, is recited, one seeks refuge from Satan, lest his whisperings come between the reciter and such purposes and acting upon them. The essential meaning is an exhortation to contemplation, directing all attention to understanding, and turning to Him (exalted is He) in every righteous deed, lest Satan corrupt it with his whisperings or come between the understanding and it. This explains the value of righteous deeds and urges sincerity in them and readiness (tashmir al-dhayl) when intending them, especially the deeds of the heart, which are the majority of what has preceded here. So He (exalted is He), addressing the most noble of His creation so that others may understand by way of priority, and so that it would be more eloquent in urging and more compelling to follow, said:

﴿So when you recite﴾, meaning: when you intend to recite, like His words, ﴿"And how many a town have We destroyed, and Our punishment came upon it"﴾ [al-A'raf: 4]; ﴿the Qur'an﴾, which is the foundation of righteous deeds, their caller and their urger, and which is also an exposition of everything. It is a generic noun, including both a little and a lot of it; ﴿then seek refuge﴾, meaning: whether aloud if you wish, or silently if you wish. Imam al-Shafi'i (may God be pleased with him) said: silence is preferable in prayer; and according to one opinion, one recites aloud as one does outside prayer; ﴿in God﴾, meaning: ask the One who possesses all perfection to protect you; ﴿from Satan﴾, meaning: the one burned by the curse; ﴿the accursed﴾, meaning: the one expelled from mercy; from his preventing you by his whisperings from following it. For there is no obstacle to submission to its excellent styles except the abandonment by the Merciful through the whisperings of Satan. So say: "I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan," for that is more fitting to the Qur'an. Some reports have come with it from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud (may God be pleased with him) as a raised (marfuʿ) narration, and it is the well-known one, and Imam al-Shafi'i (may God be pleased with him) explicitly stated it. What diverts this command from being obligatory are the many hadiths in which recitation is mentioned without any mention of seeking refuge, such as the hadith of al-Bukhari and others: "From Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla (may God be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'What prevented you from answering me?' He said: 'I was praying.' He said: 'Did not God say: ﴿O you who believe, respond to God and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]?' Then he said: 'I will surely teach you a surah that is the greatest surah in the Qur'an: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha: 2].'" And in the narration of the Muwatta': "that he (ﷺ) called Ubayy and said to him: 'How do you recite when you begin the prayer?' Ubayy said: So I recited: ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatiha: 2], until I reached its end."

Whoever examines my book "Masa'id al-Nazar li'l-Ishraf ʿala Maqasid al-Suwar" will find many such hadiths, very numerous indeed, among the finest of which is the hadith of the revelation of the surah "al-Kawthar." It was also said: seeking refuge comes after recitation, based on the apparent meaning of the verse; and the conclusion of the Qur'an with the two refuge surahs (al-Mu'awwidhatayn) agrees with this view with respect to the state (of the reciter). The first opinion, however, is the correct one with respect to what is recommended for the traveler (al-murtahil) to recite: al-Fatiha and the beginning of al-Baqara.

When that might have given the impression of exalting him, He negated it by His saying, in answer to one who seems to have asked, "Does he have authority?": ﴿Indeed, he has no authority﴾, meaning, of such a kind that the one subjected to him cannot be freed from him. ﴿Over those who believe﴾, through their Lord's granting them success. ﴿And upon their Lord﴾, meaning, Him alone, ﴿they rely﴾.

It is also permissible that the meaning is this: since it is established in minds that there is no escape from Satan, because he has been empowered over us in that he sees us from where we do not see him, and runs through us like the blood, and the benefit of seeking refuge (isti'adha) is protection (i'adha), its attainment was indicated by His saying, as a causal explanation, "Indeed, he". That is: seek refuge in Allah and He will protect you from him, because he has no authority over those who believe in Allah, so as to turn them all away from what pleases Allah, and upon their Lord alone they rely. (p-253)

Then he connected to this what had been understood from the fact that he has authority over others. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿Indeed, his authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾; that is, the authority by which he gains the utmost control, by God's granting him the ability; ﴿over those who take him as an ally﴾; that is, who made him their ally, and persisted in that by renewing his alliance at every moment; ﴿and those who, because of him, are polytheists﴾; that is, in their outward and inward states; ﴿because of him﴾; that is, because of Satan; ﴿are polytheists﴾; constantly; for when they follow his whisperings and obey his commands, they have worshipped him, and thereby made him a partner. They do not reflect on the subtleties of the Qur'an, nor even understand its apparent meanings as they truly are, because of what Satan has blinded them to through his whisperings, and what he has kept them from, by his restraints, of these methods. So they continue to disparage it with blind hearts and foul tongues.

Then he turned to this implied matter, the one indicated by the context, namely what the domination of Satan over them produced. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿And when We substitute one verse for another﴾; that is, by Our greatness, through abrogation (naskh, the annulment of a ruling by a later revelation); ﴿a verse﴾, easy, such as the waiting period of four months and ten days, and one Muslim fighting two of the disbelievers; or difficult, such as the prohibition of wine and the obligation of five prayers; ﴿and We replace it with a verse﴾, difficult, such as the waiting period of a full year and enduring ten disbelievers; or easy, such as the verses containing the permissibility of wine and the obligation of two rak'ahs at the beginning of the day and two at its end, so the second became in place of the first and a substitute for it. Or the meaning is: We abrogated a difficult verse and put in its place an easy verse. And tabdil (substitution) is the removal of a thing together with the placing of another in its stead. ﴿And Allah﴾; that is, the One who has all-encompassing knowledge; ﴿knows best what He sends down﴾; of the benefits, according to the times and circumstances, by way of abrogation or otherwise. ﴿They say﴾; that is, the disbelievers; ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾; that is, O Muhammad; meaning, you order a thing today and tomorrow you forbid it and order its opposite. But the matter is not as they say. ﴿Rather, most of them﴾; and they are those who persist in disbelief; ﴿do not know﴾; that is, knowledge does not renew itself for them; rather they are among the ranks of the beasts, because they do not benefit from the intellects Allah bestowed upon them, due to their immersion in following Satan, until their feet slipped in this clear matter after the proof of the miracle was established, namely that everything that is miraculous is from Allah, whether it is abrogating or abrogated or neither. Thus, knowing that this is the Qur'an and that is not the Qur'an, by presenting it to this proof, became one of the clearest matters and easiest to grasp for anyone among them who wished to do so, or among others, from the masters of eloquence.

So it is as if it were said: "What then shall I say?" He said: ﴿Say﴾, to those among them who confronted you with this: ﴿He has sent it down﴾, that is, the Qur'an, gradually, in accordance with the pursuit of benefits, because of the all-encompassing knowledge of the One who speaks it; ﴿the Holy Spirit﴾, who is pure spirit entirely, in whom there is no call to desire; so how could it be imagined that there is fabrication in what he brings down, especially with its attribution to the utterly pure? So he sends it down ﴿from your Lord﴾, O addressee, who has done you good by sending it down, and then by changing it according to benefits, just as He has done good in nurturing you by moving you from state to state, none of which suits what suits another: from the back to the belly, then from suckling to weaning, and what follows that. So how do you deny the changing of rulings for the sake of benefits, while not denying the changing of conditions for that reason? Such sending down is ﴿in truth﴾, that is, a firm matter, exalted above the claim of fabrication, in that it cannot be overturned; ﴿to strengthen﴾, that is, with a great strengthening, ﴿those who believe﴾ in their religion, through what they see of the miraculous nature of the substitute and the substituted despite the contrariety of the rulings, and the wisdoms and benefits within them according to those conditions, along with what was in the abrogated ruling of a similar kind according to the earlier conditions; and that they may train themselves in good submission, and it may be known, through the swiftness of their submission in abandoning what was familiar, the completeness of their surrender and the purity of their hearts from the taints of desire. Then He joined, in grammatical position with "to strengthen", His saying: ﴿and guidance﴾, that is, a clear explanation; ﴿and good news﴾, that is, through what it contains of renewing the covenant with the Supreme King and the repeated coming of the Messenger between Him and them, through the mediation of their Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, ﴿for the Muslims﴾, the submissive ones, cleared of the pride that obscures understanding and blinds the intellects. Were it not for such benefits, the wisdom of its being sent down in stages would have been lost.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 103:

When he had refuted their doubt, by allusion and expression, with what exposed them, he refuted for them another doubt, one clearer and more disgraceful than that. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿And We certainly know﴾; that is, with continuous knowledge; ﴿that they say﴾; that is, also; a repeated saying, which they never cease to utter persistently; ﴿It is only a human being who teaches him﴾; while they know that this is trivial talk. Then He resumed the response to them, so He (Exalted) said: ﴿The tongue﴾; that is, the language and speech; ﴿of the one they point to﴾; that is, they incline toward it, or they allude to it, by claiming that he taught him; ﴿is foreign﴾; that is, other than the language of the Arabs. And he, along with that, is unclear in the speech of the people of the desert; not explicit. He was a boy who had been a Christian belonging to some of the Quraysh; his name is disputed. This construction (ʿ-j-m) was established in the language of the Arabs for ambiguity and concealment, and from it comes ʿajama al-zabib (the raisin became closed), for its being hidden; and al-ʿajmaʾ (the dumb animal), for it cannot clarify what is in its self; as for ajmatu al-kitab (I removed the ambiguity from the book), it is for removal. (p-257) ﴿And this﴾; that is, the Qur'an; ﴿is a clear Arabic tongue﴾; that is, by the intensity of its clarity it shows to others that it possesses a great eloquence; so if the teacher were an Arab, it would have been necessary for them not to be unable to produce the like of what he taught; so how, when he is a foreigner?!

When their disgrace became evident through this, it was as if it were said: "It is strange that they dare to commit such a shame, while they claim to be pure and free of blemish." So He answered with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe﴾; i.e., who do not affirm with any affirmation, acknowledging ﴿the signs of Allah﴾; i.e., He to whom all greatness belongs. ﴿Allah does not guide them﴾; i.e., the Supreme King, who possesses absolute self-sufficiency; rather, He leaves them astray from the right course. Therefore they bring forth such fabrications. So give glad tidings to whoever persists greatly in obstinacy, by closing the door of understanding and rectitude.

Since it might be imagined that, because He is the one who misguides them, blame would not be directed at them, He negated that with His saying: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾; i.e., because of that, since they are the ones who engage in it, while the intended meaning is concealed from them, and power is created in them, in accordance with the customary way of some creatures with others.

When He had refuted their doubts, He affirmed for them what they had hurled at the Prophet, while he was innocent of it, restricting it to them. So He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿Only those fabricate falsehood who do not believe in the signs of God﴾; that is, they deliberately invent (yatacammadu) lies; ﴿who do not believe in the signs of God﴾; that is, faith does not renew itself among them, ﴿in the signs of God﴾; that is, the One to whom belongs all perfection. For their rejection, when the proof had been established that it is the truth, and their inability to produce its like, is a deliberate choice on their part to lie. Then He restricted the lying to them, saying: ﴿And those are the liars﴾; that is, the distant ones, the hateful ones; ﴿they are﴾; that is, exclusively; ﴿the liars﴾; that is, those who are deeply immersed in lying, outwardly and inwardly.

When He mentioned those who do not believe in general, He followed them with a category of them who are the most intense in disbelief. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿Whoever﴾, i.e., any creature who ﴿disbelieves in Allah﴾, i.e., the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, by saying or doing what indicates disbelief. Since all disbelief is harmful, even if its duration is short, He established the prepositional phrase and said: ﴿after his belief﴾, either actually or potentially, once the proofs had been established for him regarding faith, bringing him to a point where no confusion remains. So his arrogance toward faith becomes apostasy from it. The response of the conditional is indicated by what precedes it and what follows it, namely: "then he is the liar," or "upon him is wrath from Allah." ﴿Except one who has been compelled﴾, i.e., he was coerced into uttering a word of disbelief, ﴿while his heart﴾, i.e., the state being that his heart, ﴿is at rest with faith﴾, then there is nothing upon him. And they agreed, along with the permissibility of that for him, that it is not obligatory upon him to speak disbelief; rather, if he endures, that is a higher rank. The verse was revealed concerning ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with him (p-259), whom they compelled, so he followed them while he was unwilling. The Prophet (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) was informed that he had disbelieved, so the Prophet said: "Nay, indeed ʿAmmar is filled with faith from his horns to his feet, and faith has mingled with his flesh and blood." Then he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) weeping, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began wiping his eyes and saying: "If they return, then return to them with what you said." ﴿But whoever opens up with disbelief a breast﴾, i.e., opens it to the point that he begins to expand with it, i.e., from himself, or from another by being the cause of it. For the reality of faith and disbelief is tied to the heart, not the tongue; the tongue is only an expresser and interpreter, making known what is in the heart, because of the expectation of outward rulings. ﴿Upon them﴾, because of their approval of it, ﴿is wrath﴾, what a wrath! Then He explained the magnitude of it by saying ﴿from Allah﴾, i.e., the Greatest King. ﴿And for them﴾, i.e., in their outward and inward states, ﴿is a great punishment﴾, because of their apostasy upon their heels.

When those who return to the darknesses, after having come out of them into the light, are deserving of wonder, it is as if it were said: Why do they do so? Or: Why does He do that to them? So He (Exalted) said: ﴿That﴾, the apostasy, or the great threat, ﴿is because they﴾, that is, because of the fact that they, ﴿preferred﴾, that is, loved with a great love, ﴿the life of this world﴾, that is, the base, present, perishing one, and so they chose it ﴿over the Hereafter﴾, the enduring and magnificent one, because they saw what the believer has of constriction and what the disbeliever has of ease. ﴿And that﴾, that is, because ﴿Allah﴾, the King who possesses the greatest self-sufficiency, ﴿does not guide the disbelieving people﴾, those whose persistence in it He knows, but rather forsakes them and lets Satan prevail over them, so that he tricks them away from their religion.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 108:

Since their persistence in disbelief was more astonishing than their apostasy, He followed it with its cause, so He (exalted is He) said: ﴿Those﴾; that is, the remote and the hateful; ﴿those whom Allah has sealed﴾; that is, He sealed them with a seal (ṭabʿ, a sealing that is bound to bring about ruin); ﴿Allah﴾; that is, the King, with whom no one has any command; ﴿upon their hearts﴾; and since variation in hearing is rare, He made it singular, so He (exalted is He) said: ﴿and their hearing and their sights﴾; thus they became, because they derive no benefit from these faculties, as though they do not understand, nor hear, nor see; ﴿And those﴾; that is, the far removed from every good; ﴿they are the heedless﴾; that is, those who are utterly heedless.

Then He followed this with their recompense for it. He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿Undoubtedly﴾; that is, there is no doubt; ﴿that they, in the Hereafter, they are﴾; that is, specifically; ﴿the losers﴾; that is, the most complete of losers; because they lost the capital, which is their souls, so there was no return for them to return to.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 110:

When He had mentioned the one who compels (to disbelief) and the one who is compelled, He followed that with the mention of their ruling, according to the two readings. So He (Exalted is He) said, using the particle of delay (thumma), to indicate that their rank is lower than the rank of one who did not do that: ﴿Then indeed your Lord﴾; that is, the One who is good to you by pardoning your community and lightening the burdens upon them, in accepting the repentance of one who apostatized with his tongue or with his heart; ﴿for those who emigrated﴾; that is, the people of disbelief, by departing from their lands, repenting to God (Exalted is He) from what they were in;

And since He (Glorified is He) accepts a small deed at any time, He indicated this with the prepositional phrase, and so He said (Exalted is He), clarifying that trial by harm, even if severe, does not undermine emigration and what follows from it, and this implies by a fortiori reasoning that emigration without it is (even more so acceptable): ﴿after they had been tried﴾ — in the passive voice according to the reading of the majority, because what harms is the trial absolutely; and in the active voice according to the reading of Ibn 'Amir — that is, they wronged, by trying those who believed in God while they were disbelievers; or they gave the trial from themselves, so they tried them by obeying in a word of disbelief, or in returning with those who drove them back to the lands of disbelief after the emigration; ﴿after their faith﴾; ﴿then struggled﴾; that is, they carried out struggle against the disbelievers together with the Prophet (ﷺ), repenting to God (Exalted is He); ﴿and were patient﴾ upon that until they died upon it; ﴿indeed your Lord﴾; that is, the One who is good to you by subjecting to you those whose qualities are these.

And since it belongs to Him (Glorified is He) to forgive all sins except polytheism, and to punish for all of them or for some of them, and to accept all righteous deeds, and to reject some of them, He indicated this with the prepositional phrase, and so He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿after them﴾; that is, these righteous deeds occurring after those corrupt ones, which is the trial; ﴿is indeed All-Forgiving﴾; that is, abundant in erasing sins; ﴿Most Merciful﴾; that is, abundant in honoring, so He forgives them and shows them mercy.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 111:

When much of the warning and the good tidings had preceded, and it had preceded that it is not permitted for those who disbelieved to make excuse, nor will they be allowed to seek to please [their Lord], and He concluded that with the restriction of loss to the disbelievers, He made clear the Day on which those effects will appear, and described it with a description other than the one previously mentioned, in consideration of the [different] standing-places. So He (exalted is He), as a substitution for "the Day We raise up from every nation a witness" (ﷺ) said: (p-263) ﴿The Day when there comes﴾; that is, in it; ﴿every soul﴾; that is, every human being; even if its guilt is great; ﴿will argue﴾; that is, will make excuse; and He expressed it by "arguing" to convey the repelling with the utmost of what it is capable of; and He made explicit in His saying ﴿for itself﴾; that is, for its own self, alone; it is concerned with nothing else; so that the pronoun would not give the impression that every person argues on behalf of all souls. And since the requital in general is frightening and disturbing, He used the passive form in His saying ﴿and every soul will be paid in full﴾; righteous and unrighteous alike; ﴿for what it did﴾; that is, a recompense of its own kind; ﴿and they﴾; and since what is feared is absolute wrong, and the passive form is more emphatic in negating it, He (exalted is He) said: ﴿they will not be wronged﴾; that is, no wrong will be newly inflicted upon them, neither outwardly nor inwardly; so that it may be known, by the substitution of "the Day" for that preceding [phrase], that the loss lies in the establishment of the truth against them, not merely in silencing them.

(p-264) God has struck, [i.e., coined] for you, O obstinate ones, the example of a town [or city] from among the towns of the past that you know of, like the town of Hud, Salih, Lut, or Shu'ayb, peace be upon them, whose condition was like theirs. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was Makkah. ﴿It was secure﴾, meaning it had security, whereby its people were safe in a time of fear. ﴿Tranquil﴾, meaning that its people did not need to seek pasture or migrate, because of the increase in security caused by the large number of its people, the strength of its support, Allah's restraint of people from it, and the availability of what its people needed. ﴿Its provision came to it﴾, meaning continuously and steadily, ﴿abundant﴾, meaning plentiful and good, ﴿from every place﴾, by land and by sea, through Allah, exalted is He, facilitating that for them.

Since abundance often leads to arrogance (bataru), Allah, exalted is He, drew attention to this with the particle "fa" (so), and said: ﴿So it disbelieved﴾. He, glory be to Him, also drew attention to the vastness of His bounty by using the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah, the grammatical form for small numbers), which indicates that the abundance of His favor upon them is trivial compared to what He possesses, glory be to Him, the Exalted. So He said: ﴿in the blessings of Allah﴾, meaning the One to whom all perfection belongs, just as you disbelieved. ﴿So Allah made it taste﴾ (p-265), meaning the One who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, ﴿the garment of hunger﴾, after pleasant living, ﴿and fear﴾, after security and tranquility. So that becomes a garment for them, by its covering them, and by the severity of its rubbing against them it becomes a taste. The attention is directed to the borrowed-for (al-musta'ar lahu, the thing to which the metaphor is applied), and this is more eloquent here, because it indicates encompassing and tasting. Had attention been directed to the borrowed term (al-musta'ar, the metaphorical word itself), he would have said "so He clothed it," and the sense of tasting would have been lost. This is like what Kuthayyir considered in his saying:

Generous of cloak, when he smiles laughing,
the necks of wealth are shackled by his laughter.

He borrowed "cloak" for beneficence, because it protects as a cloak protects what is placed upon it, and he described it with "generous" (ghamr), which is a description of beneficence and bounty, not a description of the cloak which is the borrowed term. Had he attended to the borrowed term, he would have described it with width or length, for example, as another did, mentioning the sword with which a person protects himself:

My cloak is disputed by the servant of 'Amr,
gently, O brother of Bakr ibn 'Amr.
For me is the half that my right hand possesses,
and for you, wrap yourself with a half of it.

Here he attended to the borrowed term, which is the cloak, in the word "i'tijar" (wrapping oneself). Thus the disgrace of Ibn al-Rawandi in his heresy became evident, when he said to Ibn al-A'rabi: "Can clothing be tasted?" Ibn al-A'rabi replied to him: "Never mind, O you one-sided creature (al-nasnas). Suppose Muhammad was not a prophet; was he not an Arab?" ﴿Because of what they used to do﴾, meaning by their natures, ﴿they were doing﴾, of disbelief and arrogance, to which they had become accustomed through constant persistence, just as a person becomes accustomed to his craft.

Since God (Exalted is He) does not punish until He sends a messenger, He confirmed this with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And there had certainly come to them﴾; that is, the people of this town; ﴿a messenger from among them﴾; as happened to you; ﴿but they denied him﴾; as you did; ﴿so the punishment seized them﴾; as you have heard. And if by it is meant Makkah, then what is meant is the famine, for which the Prophet (ﷺ) invoked against them when he said: "O Allah, help me against them with seven [years] like the seven [years] of Joseph." As for the fear, it was not from the jihad of the Prophet (ﷺ) against them; ﴿while they were wrongdoers﴾; that is, excessive in placing things in other than their proper places, because they persisted in their disbelief despite the hunger, and they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for relief, so he supplicated for them.

When al-Tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness) had been established by the proofs that preceded it, it became firmly settled, beyond any doubt, that God alone is the (sole) deity, just as He alone is the Provider. He also drew their attention to subtle details in His apportioning of sustenance, which point to His greatness, the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, His power, and His choice. Thus it was established that they were wrong in what they assigned to the idols of His provision, and that no one may move except by His command, glory be to Him. He concluded this with the parable that warns against ingratitude for blessings, and he followed it with His words (exalted is He), turning them away from the practices of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance): ﴿So eat﴾; that is, as a consequence of all that has passed, it is said to them: eat; ﴿of what God has provided for you﴾; that is, the One who possesses majesty and beauty; of what He has counted for you in this surah and in others; ﴿lawful and good﴾ (while being) such that there is no doubt in it and no impediment in any respect; ﴿and be grateful for the blessing of God﴾; that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection; out of caution lest He bring upon you what He brought upon the town that was used as the example; ﴿if it is Him alone that you worship﴾; that is, Him alone, ﴿as these proofs require﴾, for He alone is the One who provides for you; otherwise He would hasten punishment upon you, for after obstinacy in the face of clear proof there is nothing but retribution. Thus the discourse concerning provision and the rebuke for not being grateful encompasses the parables both before and after.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 115:

(p-268) Since the permission is only for some of the sustenance, in the state mentioned, it was necessary to know it. The permitted things are more numerous than the forbidden ones, so He confined the few so that the many might be known from it, because when two known opposites are described in general terms, specifying one of them makes the other known from its specification. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿Indeed, He has forbidden for you carrion﴾; that is, God, to whom no one has any command beside Him; ﴿carrion﴾, which was explained by the tongue of the Messenger, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to be carrion even if it was slaughtered (dhakkā, properly slaughtered); ﴿and blood and the flesh of swine﴾. He singled it out for mention after its inclusion in carrion because the Christians have taken eating it as a matter of religion; ﴿and that over which other than God has been invoked﴾; that is, with whatever invocation it was, from whatever one invoked it. Since the purpose of the surah is to demonstrate perfection, it was more fitting to mention "other than" first, to make ugly the state of the one who is devoted to it. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿to other than God﴾; that is, the Greatest King, who has no king besides Him; ﴿by it﴾.

Since a person may be compelled to eat anything that can be eaten, He made clear to them that He was gentle with them, and permitted them to ward off hunger with what is forbidden. So He (Exalted) said: ﴿But whoever is compelled﴾; that is, however the compulsion befalls him; ﴿neither desiring [it] nor transgressing﴾, against another who is compelled; ﴿nor exceeding﴾ the bare minimum needed to ward off hunger.

Since the permission to eat these things in the state of necessity (p-269) is only a concession (rukhṣa, a legal dispensation), and since desire calls toward what goes beyond what is permitted, He (Exalted) said: ﴿Indeed God﴾; that is, the One singularly characterized by the attributes of perfection; ﴿is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward the one who takes from them in the manner He has set limits for. As for whoever exceeds what he has been permitted, he is deserving of retribution.

When, by this verse (as its explanation was already given in al-Anʿām), the entire category of animals whose eating is forbidden had become clear, their ignorance regarding what they had prohibited for themselves for the sake of their idols became known. So He explicitly forbade it, as a further emphasis on that restriction. He (exalted) said: ﴿And do not say﴾, i.e., in any manner, at any time.

Since their declaring things lawful and unlawful was an empty statement with no reality at all, for it had no evidence, He described it as an attribute uttered by the tongue, one that does not deserve to enter the heart. He (exalted) said: ﴿for what your tongues describe﴾, i.e., on account of what you describe, ﴿your tongues﴾, i.e., concerning the livestock, the tillage, and the crops. Since this stirred the soul to know what is said on account of that, He clarified the content of that saying, saying (exalted): ﴿the lie﴾, i.e., the saying which is the very essence of falsehood.

Since the eagerness to identify that content intensified, He put in apposition to it: ﴿"This is lawful and this is unlawful."﴾ It is possible that "the lie" is the object of "describe", so that "mā" (in "limā") is a verbal particle (maṣdariyya), meaning: because of their describing it. This would be as if the reality of the lie were unknown, so it was not recognized except through their tongues' description of it. This is hyperbole in describing their speech as lying, and what follows it is the content of the saying.

Since they, as previously mentioned, claimed to be the most intelligent of people, it was fitting for them, as a loosening of the rein, to be attributed with knowledge of the necessary consequences when undertaking the things that necessitate them. He (exalted) said: ﴿that you may fabricate against Allah﴾, i.e., the Supreme King, ﴿the lie﴾. For whoever attributes to anyone what that person has not permitted, his statement is a lie, and his lying is for the purpose of fabricating a lie; otherwise he would be in utter ignorance. So their situation in such matters revolves between extreme stupidity or intending what no intelligent person would intend, and this is a wondrous kind of mockery. It is as if it were said: "What do they deserve for that?" He answered with His saying (exalted): ﴿Indeed, those who fabricate against Allah, i.e., deliberately invent, ﴾ ﴿the lie﴾ ﴿against Allah, i.e., the One to whom all command belongs, ﴾ ﴿the lie﴾, whether from you or from others, ﴿will not prosper.﴾

Since success, in their view, is a wide ease of living in this world, he answered one who seemed to say: "So we see them enjoying blessing and comfort." Thus He (Exalted) said: ﴿A little enjoyment﴾; that is, what they are in is little, because it perishes, even if it extends for a thousand years; ﴿and for them﴾ after it ﴿is a painful punishment﴾; and of its great pain is that it is everlasting. So what kind of enjoyment is this?!

ولَمّا بَيَّنَ لَهم نِعْمَتَهُ بِتَوْسِعَتِهِ عَلَيْهِمْ؛ بِما ضَيَّقُوا بِهِ عَلى أنْفُسِهِمْ؛ بَيَّنَ لَهم نِعْمَةً أُخْرى؛ بِتَمْيِيزِهِمْ عَلى بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ؛ فَقالَ (تَعالى): (p-٢٧١)﴿وعَلى الَّذِينَ هادُوا﴾؛ أيْ: اليَهُودِ؛ ﴿حَرَّمْنا﴾؛ أيْ: بِعَظَمَتِنا؛ عُقُوبَةً لَهُمْ؛ بِعُدْوانِهِمْ؛ وكَذِبِهِمْ عَلى رَبِّهِمْ؛ ﴿ما قَصَصْنا﴾؛ أيْ: بِما لَنا مِنَ العَظَمَةِ؛ الَّتِي كانَ المَقْصُوصُ بِها مُعْجِزًا؛ ﴿عَلَيْكَ﴾

ولَمّا لَمْ يَكُنْ قَصُّ ذَلِكَ عَلَيْهِ - صَلّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وعَلى آلِهِ وسَلَّمَ - مُسْتَغْرِقًا زَمانَ القَبْلِ؛ أدْخَلَ الجارَّ؛ فَقالَ: ﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾؛ أيْ: في ”الأنْعامِ“؛ ﴿وما ظَلَمْناهُمْ﴾؛ أيْ: الَّذِينَ وقَعَ مِنهُمُ الهَوْدُ؛ بِتَحْرِيمِنا عَلَيْهِمْ ما حَرَّمْنا؛ ﴿ولَكِنْ كانُوا﴾؛ أيْ: دائِمًا؛ طَبْعًا لَهُمْ؛ وخُلُقًا مُسْتَمِرًّا؛ ﴿أنْفُسَهُمْ﴾؛ أيْ: خاصَّةً؛ ﴿يَظْلِمُونَ﴾؛ أيْ: بِالبَغْيِ؛ والكُفْرِ؛ فَضَيَّقْنا عَلَيْهِمْ مُعامَلَةً بِالعَدْلِ؛ وعامَلْناكم أنْتُمْ - حَيْثُ ظَلَمْتُمْ - بِالفَضْلِ؛ فاشْكُرُوا النِّعْمَةَ؛ واحْذَرُوا غَوائِلَ النِّقْمَةِ.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 119:

When he had explained this worldly blessing, he followed it with a blessing that is far greater than it, in order to attract every wrongdoer; and he showed its greatness by the particle of delayed sequence (ḥarf al-tarākhī). So He (exalted be He) said: ﴿Then indeed your Lord﴾; that is, the One who does good to you; ﴿for those who did evil﴾; and evil (sū') is everything that is by its nature bad, that which it is not fitting to do; ﴿in ignorance﴾; as you did, even if their deed was great and their ignorance was gross; ﴿then repented﴾. And since He (glory be to Him) accepts even a small deed, He introduced the preposition, so He said (exalted be He): ﴿after that﴾; that is, after the sin, even if it was great; so they restricted themselves to what their Creator permitted; ﴿and amended﴾; by persisting in that; ﴿indeed your Lord﴾; that is, the One who does good to you by facilitating your religion and making it easy. And since He forgives after repentance only what lies beyond shirk that occurs after it, He introduced the preposition, so He said (exalted be He): ﴿after it﴾; that is, after the repentance, and [He forgives] what preceded it of evil deeds; ﴿surely Oft-Forgiving﴾; that is, most thorough in covering what they did of evil; ﴿Most Merciful﴾; that is, the One who bestows favor through honoring, as bounty and blessing.

When he called them to noble character and forbade them from its vices, by accepting whoever came to him, however grave his sin, in response to the call of their father Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when he said: ﴿So whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Ibrahim: 36], He followed that with a mention of him, to encourage following him in monotheism (tawhid, the affirmation of God's oneness), and in inclining with the command and the prohibition, advancing and withdrawing, if they were among those who follow the truth or who imitate their fathers. So He said, by way of giving the reason for what preceded it: ﴿Indeed Ibrahim﴾, that is, your greatest father, the leader of the monotheists, ﴿was a nation﴾. In him were worldly and otherworldly benefits that make it necessary that everyone who can benefit from him should aim for him and seek him out. ﴿Devoted﴾, that is, sincere, ﴿to God﴾, that is, the King to whom all command belongs, having nothing of caprice in him; ﴿upright﴾ (ḥanīf, inclining steadfastly toward the truth), inclining with the command and the prohibition, whether by abrogation (naskh, the replacing of one ruling by a later one) or otherwise. So be upright, followers of the truth, (p-273) according to the proofs that stand upon it, and emulating the best of your fathers.

Since the context is to establish perfection for Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and the affirmative attributes are near to grasp and quick to reach understanding, and after them came a negative attribute in a single clause, He dropped the nun of "yakun" (the verb "to be") from it, for brevity and to bring it closer to understanding, lightening it for the listener, and to keep him from going, before its completion, to other than the intended meaning, and to inform that the act is negated of him (peace be upon him) in the most emphatic forms of negation, such that nothing of it is attributed to him, even a little. So it was said: ﴿and he was not﴾. And since they, and many of their ancestors, were polytheists, He censured them for that, since the greatest of their fathers whose greatness they believe in is not of that kind. So He (exalted is He) said: ﴿of the polytheists﴾, those who stand with caprice. So do not be of them.

Then He described his state, saying: ﴿grateful﴾. And since Allah has countless blessings toward the one He made into an ummah (a community unto himself), He showed that all of that is little compared to His bounty. He said, pointing to this with the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah), ﴿for His blessings﴾; and to indicate that one who gives thanks for little gives thanks when much comes to him by way of a fortiori reasoning (min bab al-awla): ﴿He is ever giving more of His bounty to him; so He accepted his supplication for you (p-274) — so be thankful to Allah, following his example, that He may increase you.﴾ It is as if it were said: What did He reward him with for that? Or he gave the reason for what came before, so He (exalted is He) said: ﴿He chose him﴾, that is, He selected him with complete selection; ﴿and guided him﴾, that is, with the greatest clarification and the most perfect divine success; ﴿to a straight path﴾, which is the tolerant, upright monotheism (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah). Thus he was among those who enjoin justice, and he was upon a straight path, and he was the opposite of the mute man described in the preceding parable.

And We gave him good in this world; [He said:] (Q. 16:122) "And We gave him in this world good." (Al-Biqa'i glosses this, and the phrase "li-sān al-ṣidq" with its own reference.)

Let me correct that: here is the faithful translation.

Then He said: ﴿And We gave him﴾; that is, with what We possess of greatness; ﴿in this world﴾; with a tongue of truthfulness and a beautiful praise, by which We made the tongues of creation submissive to him; ﴿good﴾. He alluded, by expressing the Giver with the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama), to His exaltedness, since He made him a revered imam for all the adherents of the religious communities (milal); so He gathered hearts upon love for him, and made for him among them a tongue of truthfulness; and He granted him, in his progeny, prophethood, righteousness, dominion, and abundance, which are well known.

And since the greatness of this world is not considered except when accompanied by the blessing of the Hereafter, He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter﴾; and He said (Exalted is He): ﴿among the righteous﴾; that is, he has what they have of great reward; expressing it with "min" (among), to magnify the station of righteousness and to encourage toward it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 123:

When he had established, regarding his greatness in this world and the Hereafter, that which calls to following him, he stated the command to follow him explicitly, as an alert to the increase in his greatness, by a matter far removed in rank from the other attributes with which He praised him. That matter is that he became the exemplar (muqtada) of the most excellent of the children of Adam, indicating this by the particle of delayed sequence (harf al-taraakhi), which indicates the loftiness of his rank, by the loftiness of the rank of the one whom He commanded to be followed in what He laid down for him of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and the clear, easy path. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Then We revealed to you﴾; that is: then We increased him in exaltation and majesty by revealing to him, ﴿to you﴾, and you are the most noble of creation. He explained the revelation by His saying, mighty and majestic is He, encouraging the reception of this revelation in the best manner of reception, by following the great father: ﴿that follow﴾; that is: with the utmost of your effort and the ultimate of your resolve.

Since the intended thing is the root of the religion, and the good manner of its demand, with ease of submission and withdrawal from all falsehood, and calling with gentleness, together with patience, repeated presentation of the proofs, and everything to which pure reason and sound nature call, He expressed it by the term "religion" (millah), so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿the religion of Abraham﴾; and there is no remoteness in this making understood the migration (hijrah) as well.

Since the hanifiyyah (pure monotheism) was the most noble of the moral qualities of Abraham, peace be upon him, and it was intended in itself, He stated it explicitly, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿a hanif﴾; that is: in the state of your being, or his being one of strong inclination together with the true proof. And He encouraged the Arabs toward tawhid and repelled them from shirk by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾; that is: in any way whatsoever.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 124:

When He, glory be to Him, had called in it (the surah) to lofty character and to refraining from objection, and concluded with the command to follow the upright religion (al-millah al-hanifiyyah), which is ease of submission to proof and not being among the rigid adherents (al-jamidin), following the Greatest Father (Abraham, peace be upon him), and since dispute and hardship contradict his religion and do not lead to any good, and since it is known that every ruling that came after him is not part of his religion, and since the Jews, out of ignorance, claimed that he was upon their religion, and the Sabbath was among the greatest of their rites, this produced His saying (exalted is He), as an answer to whoever among the Jews might claim that he was upon their religion, and as a warning against punishment for disagreeing about the truth, by way of severity in the matter: ﴿Verily, the Sabbath was only made﴾, i.e., by the making of One who has no command over Him by anyone else, ﴿the Sabbath﴾, i.e., its prohibition and its sanctity, or its burden, ﴿for those who differed concerning it﴾, when their prophet commanded them to (observe) Friday, so some of them accepted that, while others wanted the Sabbath, and so they replaced Friday with the Sabbath. He made it severe for them in its matter as retribution against them, by what the transitive use with "ʿalā" (upon) conveys, so that became a burden upon them. In this is a reminder of the blessing of ease upon us.

Al-Baghawi said: al-Kalbi said: Musa (peace be upon him) commanded them concerning Friday and said: "Devote yourselves to God one day in every seven days; worship Him on Friday, and do not do any of your craft-work on it, and (work) six days for your crafts." But they refused, except for a small group among them, and said: "We want only the day on which God finished creation, which is Saturday." So that day was made incumbent upon them and was made severe for them in it. Then ʿIsa (peace be upon him) came to them with Friday, and they said: "We do not want their festival to come after our festival," so they took Sunday. Then God gave Friday to this community, and they accepted it, and blessing was given to them in it.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq said in his tafsir: Maʿmar informed me, someone who heard Mujahid informed me, saying concerning His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Verily, the Sabbath was only made﴾: "They rejected Friday and took the Sabbath in its place."

Al-Shaykhan narrated from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We are the last (in the world) and the first on the Day of Resurrection, though they were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them. This is their day which God made obligatory upon them, but they differed concerning it, so God guided us to it, and they are following us in it: the Jews tomorrow, and the Christians the day after tomorrow."

Since association (shirk) was clear in the matter of the Christians, He dispensed with explicitly stating that it (the Sabbath) is not upon their religion by negating it, then He warned against disagreement, affirming the matter of resurrection, so He said (exalted is He): ﴿And indeed your Lord﴾, i.e., the one who does good to you by the obedience of your companions to you; ﴿will judge between them﴾, i.e., these (p-278) disputants; ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, when all creatures are gathered; ﴿concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾, i.e., by their natural dispositions, ﴿about the acceptance of Friday and its rejection, and about submitting to the prohibition of hunting and refusing it, and other matters﴾; so each party among them will be recompensed according to what it deserves.

[p-279] When He, glory be to Him, had earlier in this surah recounted much of their mockery of His promise and His threat, and their denial of His messengers, in the most hideous manner, along with the intensity of His Messenger's concern for them, which led to deep grief over their misguidance, and other things that might have caused him to despair of them and withdraw from calling them, He followed this with the coining of parables and the presenting of disputation. These are among the inimitable methods, whose outward meanings, when heard, first bring to understanding sublime meanings and beautiful purposes that are beyond description for the common people. When the elite contemplate them, they find in them subtle realities, paths of refined truths, firm proofs, and well-crafted aims and means. These make clear, through the differing of understandings and the variety of thoughts, that it is a sea with no shore, no bottom, and no end to what the gaze extracts from it. Having concluded with the following of the Greatest Father, and since all of this was so, God, glory be to Him, commanded His Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, who is the one who hears and obeys, to follow his traces and to take as a model his inward and outward conduct. He then explained to him the creed (millah) which He had commanded him to follow, and said, exalted is He: ﴿Invite﴾, that is, everyone whose invitation is possible, ﴿to the way of your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you, by facilitating the way to which you call and making it broad, and it is Islam, which is the upright creed (al-millah al-hanifiyyah); ﴿with wisdom﴾ (hikmah, here meaning that which makes known the ranks of actions in goodness and ugliness, righteousness and corruption). It was called "hikmah" because it acts as a preventive against corruption and against what should not be chosen. Thus the wise (hakim) is the one who knows what prevents corruption, as stated by al-Rummani. In reality it is clear truth, so whoever is fit for it is called with it. ﴿And good admonition﴾ (al-mawʿizah), by means of parables, promise and threat, mixing desire with dread, and warning with glad tidings; ﴿good﴾, that is, whose outward meaning is easily grasped by every understanding, and whose inward contents delight every skilled person, together with gentleness in its aim and in its delivery, for those who can bear only this. ﴿And argue with them﴾, that is, with those among them who can bear that, turn them away from their false creeds to your true creed by way of argument; ﴿in the way that is best﴾ among the methods, with gentleness, softness, dignity and tranquility. And do not turn away from them in despair, nor requite them for their evil speech and ugly deeds, but pardon them and be gentle with them. This is an explanation of the kinds of calling according to the intellects of those called, because the prophets, upon them be peace, are commanded to address people according to the measure of their intellects. It has been said: if the calling is for establishing the religion and confirming belief in the hearts of its adherents, and it is with that certain and purified from any possibility of the opposite, then it is wisdom, which is for the seeker of truth who submits, if he is prepared to accept it with his penetrating thought. If it is accompanied by the possibility of the opposite, yielding conjecture and persuasion, then it is admonition, which is for the one who submits but has no readiness. If it is for obliging the deniers and silencing the obstinate, then it is disputation (jadal). If it is composed of premises accepted by the majority or by the opponent alone, then it is the "good" (hasanah). If it is composed of false premises not accepted, aimed at promoting them through false tricks and corrupt methods, then it is the "bad" (sayyi'ah), which does not befit the fair-minded. Then He gave the reason for the necessity of calling them in this manner, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you by lightening your burden, ﴿He﴾, that is, alone, ﴿knows best﴾, that is, more than anyone who might be supposed to have knowledge, ﴿who has strayed from His way﴾, so that he is in the lowest degrees of misguidance, and He knows best those who go astray, who are firmly rooted in deviating from the path, [p-281] so there is no escape for him from misguidance; ﴿and He knows best who is guided to His way﴾, so that he is in the lowest degrees of guidance. ﴿And He﴾, that is, alone, ﴿knows best the guided﴾, that is, those who are at the very height of it. So the verse is of the type called ihtibak (a device in which elements are omitted on each side that are indicated by their counterparts): He first mentioned "those who have strayed," as an indication of the omission of their opposite in the second part, and "the guided" in the second part as an indication of the omission of their opposite in the first part.

As for you, you have no knowledge of any of that except by Our informing you. We have obligated you to clear conveyance, so do not slacken in it, turning away out of destructive eagerness or despair, for it is not upon you to guide them.

Now that he [the author] has explained the matter of the call (*da'wah*, the invitation to Islam) and clarified its methods, and has presented the matter of emigration (*hijrah*), compulsion in religion, and the trials connected with it, pointing out the tribulations and afflictions that the disbelievers inflicted through injustice, and has concluded all of that with the command to show gentleness toward them, he generalized it. After [the Prophet], may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, had been singled out for the command of gentleness, he commanded his followers to act with justice and kindness, as has already been mentioned, even toward the worst of enemies, and forbade them to requite them except in the manner of justice. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you retaliate﴾; that is, if you come to have an opportunity to retaliate against them, by which you are able to inflict harm upon them; ﴿then retaliate with the like of that with which you were afflicted﴾. Since the command applies generally to every act of retaliation, from whatever agent it proceeds, and since the identity of the agent is not of any concern, He formed the verb in the passive, saying: ﴿you were afflicted﴾. In this, according to the customary usage of kings in their speech, there is an indication of their being overcome by the enemy, and of their Islam [being] in their hands, and the placing of it with the particle of doubt establishes a balance between fear and hope.

Since He had permitted them the degree of justice, He raised them to the rank of kindness, by His saying: ﴿And if you endure patiently﴾, by pardoning them; ﴿it is indeed﴾, that is, patience; ﴿better for the patient﴾. He used the apparent noun in the place where a pronoun would be expected, for generality and to attach the judgment to the attribute.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 16, verse 127:

Since the implied sense was "so be patient," he (exalted is He) joined to it, by singling him out, the command addressed to him (ﷺ), out of honour for him and as consolation for what was the occasion of the revelation of the verse, namely the mutilation of his paternal uncle Hamzah (may Allah be pleased with him). It also emphasises the great rank of patience, to increase the exhortation to the community, because a command from the leader is more effective in prompting his followers to comply. So He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And be patient﴾. Then He followed this with what urges the constant turning to Him, which produces muraqabah (inner vigilance before Allah) and fana' (annihilation of attention to other than Allah), and then fana' 'an al-fana' (annihilation from annihilation itself), lest it be supposed that anyone has an independent act. So He said: ﴿And your patience is not but through Allah﴾. That is, O Messenger, the greatest [p. 283], ﴿not but through Allah﴾, that is, the Greatest King, who prescribed for you this most upright law, while you stand in His support.

He (ﷺ) met this command with the highest degrees of patience. This is because they mutilated the corpses of the Muslims at the Battle of Uhud, except Handhalah al-Ghasil (may Allah be pleased with him), whose father was with them, so they left him for him. When the Prophet (ﷺ) stood over his uncle Hamzah (may Allah be pleased with him) and found that they had slit his nose, cut off his ears, castrated him, and ripped open his belly, he looked at a sight more painful to his heart than any he had ever seen. He said: "May Allah have mercy on you, for you were a doer of good and one who maintained the ties of kinship. Were it not that Safiyyah would grieve, I would have been pleased to leave you until you are gathered from the bellies of beasts. By Allah, if Allah grants me victory over them, I will mutilate seventy of them." The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) said: "We will surely exceed what they have done." When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) hastened to comply. He never delivered a sermon without forbidding mutilation, and on the day of the Conquest he showed kindness by forgiving them after they had come under his power (ﷺ), and he was honoured, exalted, revered, and glorified, forever and ever.

When, after settling the soul to patience and emptying the heart of resentment, there remained a sorrow over their destruction of themselves through their persistence in rebellion against Allah (exalted is He), He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, that is, over the severity of their disbelief, so that you would exceed in an eager concern that consumes the soul.

When He, glorified is He, was at the station of giving glad tidings, at a great place and a momentous station, which no bringer of good tidings or warner had attained before our Prophet (ﷺ), and that is the Isra' (the Night Journey) to the highest dominion and the loftiest station among the lofty heavens, in the presences of holiness (hadarat al-qudus) and places of intimacy, and He prepared for that in the surah of blessings with stations of generosity, until arrival at it drew near, He abbreviated the expression by omitting a letter that is not needed, as a sign pointing to it. So He said: ﴿And do not be﴾, with the nun removed, indicating that the situation is too constricted for even the slightest extension:

Longing is at its most intense, one day,
when the abodes draw near to the abodes.

This is unlike what comes in surah "al-Naml" (surah 27), God willing: ﴿in distress﴾, even if slight, as the diminutive nunation (tanwin al-tahqir, the nunation expressing belittlement) hints, by what the omission of the nun points to. For the harm of the disbelievers, from which the context is consoling you, does not harm you in the purpose for which you were sent, which is the manifestation of the religion and the suppression of the corrupters in some way. ﴿Of what they scheme﴾, that is, from their continual scheming against you. ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Hijr: 99], as though you already see it, and it has come. So be patient, for Allah (exalted is He) will strengthen you and make your religion prevail, even if they dislike it.

ثُمَّ عَلَّلَ ذَلِكَ بِقَوْلِهِ (تَعالى): ﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ ("Indeed, Allah"); أيْ: الجامِعَ لِصِفاتِ الكَمالِ؛ بِلُطْفِهِ؛ وعَوْنِهِ؛ ﴿مَعَ الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا﴾ ("is with those who have taqwa (God-consciousness)"); أيْ: وُجِدَ مِنهُمُ الخَوْفُ مِنَ اللَّهِ (تَعالى)؛ فَكانُوا في أوَّلِ مَنازِلِ التَّقْوى؛ وهو مَعَ المُتَّقِينَ الَّذِينَ كانُوا في النِّهايَةِ مِنها؛ فَعَدَلُوا في أفْعالِهِمْ مِنَ التَّوْحِيدِ (tawhid, affirming the oneness of God) وغَيْرِهِ؛ عَمَلًا بِأمْرِ اللَّهِ في الكِتابِ؛ الَّذِي هو تِبْيانٌ لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ؛ وهو مَعَ الَّذِينَ أحْسَنُوا؛ وكانُوا في أوَّلِ دَرَجاتِ الإحْسانِ (ihsan, excellence in worship and conduct)؛ ﴿والَّذِينَ هُمْ﴾ ("and those who")؛ أيْ: بِضَمائِرِهِمْ؛ وظَواهِرِهِمْ؛ ﴿مُحْسِنُونَ﴾ ("are doers of good")؛ أيْ: صارَ الإحْسانُ صِفَةً لَهم غَيْرَ مُنْفَكَّةٍ عَنْهُمْ؛ فَهم في حَضَراتِ الرَّحْمَنِ؛ وأنْتَ رَأْسُ المُتَّقِينَ المُحْسِنِينَ؛ فاللَّهُ مَعَكَ؛ ومَن كانَ اللَّهُ مَعَهُ كانَ غالِبًا؛ وصَفْقَتُهُ رابِحَةٌ؛ وحالَتُهُ صالِحَةٌ؛ وأمْرُهُ عالٍ؛ وضِدُّهُ في أسْوَإ الأحْوالِ؛ فَلا تَسْتَعْجِلُوا قَلَقًا؛ كَما اسْتَعْجَلَ الكُفّارُ اسْتِهْزاءً؛ تَخَلُّقًا في التَّأنِّي والحِلْمِ بِصِفَةِ مَن تَنَزَّهَ عَنْ نَقْصِ الِاسْتِعْجالِ؛ وتَعالى عَنِ ادِّعاءِ الأكْفاءِ والأمْثالِ؛ فَقَدْ عانَقَ آخِرُها أوَّلَها؛ ووافَقَ مَقْطَعُها مَطْلَعَها؛ وآخِرُها احْتِباكٌ (ihtibak, a rhetorical device in which two elements are each omitted from one clause and mentioned in the other): ذَكَرَ ”الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا“؛ أوَّلًا؛ دَلِيلًا عَلى حَذْفِ ”الَّذِينَ أحْسَنُوا“؛ ثانِيًا؛ والمُحْسِنِينَ ثانِيًا؛ دَلِيلًا عَلى حَذْفِ المُتَّقِينَ أوَّلًا؛ واللَّهُ المُوَفِّقُ لِلصَّوابِ؛ وإلَيْهِ المَرْجِعُ والمَآبُ.
